Renewable fuels or CCS? Identifying drivers in net-zero transport and energy systems
abstract: Deep emission reductions in heavy transport sectors, such as long-distance aviation and shipping, require either large-scale substitution toward renewable fuels or continued fossil use compensated by carbon capture and sequestration. While renewable fuels rely on scarce resources including renewable electricity, hydrogen, and biomass, compensation of fossil emissions is constrained by the cost and availability of CO₂ capture and the capacity for transport and sequestration. This study applies the sector-coupled energy system model Balmorel-OptiFlow to identify least-cost strategies for achieving a net-zero energy system in Western Europe by 2050. By endogenously optimising transport fuel supply and carbon management across multiple CO₂ value chains, and applying a one-at-a-time sensitivity analysis, the study identifies conditions under which the fuel mix shifts between renewable and fossil fuels. Biofuel deployment scales directly with biomass availability, whereas electrofuels are deployed only when low-cost electricity and hydrogen, or high fossil fuel prices, make them competitive with fossil pathways compensated by carbon capture and sequestration. Even under high renewable fuel uptake, carbon management remains central to the least-cost system, with 145–402 MtCO₂/yr sequestration across scenarios, driven by persistent fossil energy use in aviation and industrial heat.

An advanced optimization framework for offshore wind farm layout design
abstract: : A well-designed wind farm layout can effectively mitigate wake effects and improve wind farm power generation. This study presents an engineering-oriented wind farm layout optimization (WFLO) framework integrating the cosine wake model with the genetic random search algorithm. The cosine wake model is evaluated against other wake models and demonstrates improved power prediction accuracy. The genetic random search algorithm achieves superior optimization performance compared with other algorithms in a benchmark study. The present framework is further investigated in three case studies. Each case is executed independently for 30 runs to ensure reliable performance assessment. The statistical results from a benchmark case indicate that the choice of the inner optimization time has little practical effect on optimization performance. For the Horns Rev wind farm, the present framework achieves a 1.25% improvement in annual energy production (AEP), outperforming the layout reported in the literature and the sequential least squares programming (SLSQP) solution. For the offshore wind farm sites near Shenzhen, the present framework also consistently outperforms the SLSQP solver, achieving AEP improvements of up to 2.11% and 4.31% at the Mirs Bay and Pearl River Estuary sites, respectively. The multi-start approach proves essential for generating feasible layouts for high-density wind farm sites under the minimum turbine spacing constraint. Statistical evaluations based on the real-world case studies demonstrate the superior optimization performance, robustness, and reliability of the present framework. The optimal layouts obtained in this study could serve as valuable references for future WFLO cross-comparison studies.

abstract: Integration of an auxiliary heat pump into a transcritical carbon dioxide heating system provides an effective solution for managing high return-water temperatures in district heating applications, where conventional carbon dioxide heat pumps experience significant performance degradation. However, system performance is strongly affected by thermodynamic interactions between the auxiliary and carbon dioxide subsystems, requiring simultaneous optimization of multiple operating and design parameters. Existing studies have mainly optimized individual variables, such as discharge pressure or intermediate water temperature, rather than the complete integrated configuration. This study addresses this limitation by conducting a comprehensive system-level optimization using a fast and elitist Single-Objective Genetic Algorithm to simultaneously optimize operating pressures, temperature levels, and flow distribution to maximize the coefficient of performance. Six refrigerants namely isobutane, 1,1,1,2-tetrafluoroethane, 2,3,3,3-tetrafluoropropene, ammonia, 1,1-difluoroethane, and propane were evaluated as working fluids for the auxiliary heat pump. Isobutane achieved the highest system performance, followed by ammonia and 1,1,1,2-tetrafluoroethane. System performance was strongly influenced by the selected design variables, which required careful balancing to maximize the coefficient of performance. For most refrigerants, the optimal temperature reduction across the auxiliary evaporator ranged from 11.0 to 12.3 °C, whereas isobutane and 1,1,1,2-tetrafluoroethane achieved optimal performance at approximately 15 °C. The optimum total and split water flow rates directed to the carbon dioxide loop were approximately 7 kg/s and 2.9–3.25 kg/s, respectively. The results confirm that integrating auxiliary heat recovery with comprehensive multi-variable optimization reduced the power consumption of the parallel compression system by approximately 39.8% and improved the coefficient of performance from 1.83 to approximately 3.04.

The operational flexibility and thermodynamic performance evaluation of wide-range dry state supercritical coal-fired power plants
abstract: ABSTRACT Enhancing the operational flexibility of supercritical coal-fired power plants (CFPPs) under deep peak-shaving scenarios is important for grid stability and renewable energy accommodation. However, the inevitable wet state operation has emerged as the critical bottleneck restricting ultra-low load regulation potential. In this regard, comparisons between wet and dry states were conducted for a 660 MW unit, including thermodynamic performance, spatiotemporal distribution of energy/exergy storage, and dynamic response characteristics. Results reveal that the qualitative degradation of energy storage constitutes the primary cause behind the insufficient ramp-up potential operating at the wet state. Despite storing more energy at low-temperature heating surfaces, its theoretical potential to produce useful work stands at a mere 36.1% of the scale observed in the high-temperature counterparts. Under typical step disturbances, the maximum output power increase is attenuated by 5.7 MW compared to the dry state. To overcome these constraints, the wide-range dry state systems based on internal thermodynamic potential exploitation were proposed, encompassing direct and ejector-driven heating schemes. The overall exergy quality of the energy storage is upgraded by minimizing the boiler inlet subcooling degree. Performance evaluation shows that when adopting proposed systems, the load ramp-up rates can be augmented by 7.7 MW/min at most, exceeding 2.5% Pe/min at a peak-shaving depth of over 80%, while increasing cumulative electricity generation up to 2708.9 MJ. The associated energy consumption penalty can be mitigated through the ejector-driven schemes by approximately 0.50 g/kWh, to 0.71 g/kWh. This study offers a forward-looking reference for supercritical CFPPs under the new operating paradigm.

A multifunctional thermal management design for lithium-ion batteries operating at different temperatures
abstract: ABSTRACT The widespread use of lithium-ion batteries (LIBs) is increasingly challenged by their vulnerability to thermal conditions, particularly when directly exposed to adverse or dynamically varying environments. To address this issue, a multifunctional battery thermal management (BTM) design is proposed, integrating phase change materials (PCMs), thermoelectric modules (TEMs) and heat pipes (HPs), with HPs bridging TEMs and LIBs to facilitate direct heat transfer. The design employs PCM phase change as the primary cooling means, supplemented by TEM-refrigeration for high-temperature scenarios. Meanwhile, it utilizes solidified PCM to mitigate heat loss from batteries under sub-zero conditions and applies TEM-heating to preheat LIBs before cold starts. Experiments were conducted by discharging NCM prismatic batteries with the proposed design under continuous and pulsed profiles across various thermal conditions. At the ambient temperatures and , the maximum battery-surface temperatures successfully remained within ; the maximum temperature differences were less than . Under the high-temperature circumstance, TEM-refrigeration outperformed both air- and liquid-cooling in identical continuous discharge and input power conditions. At , solidified PCM effectively prevented a plunge in battery temperatures, and TEM-heating achieved a preheating rate of . It is also revealed that the proposed BTM design can electrically control TEM on-off through a set of logic rules, enabling instantaneous regulation of the battery temperature rise and distribution in response to ambient temperature surges and drops. All these findings demonstrate the superior efficacy of the proposed BTM design, whose multifunctional capabilities, including cooling, insulation and preheating, can fulfil diverse thermal requirements of LIBs in various conditions.

Convective heat transfer optimization for liquid cooling plates driven by field synergy and fractal geometry
abstract: The rapid development of liquid-cooled data centers has imposed imperative demands on the performance of liquid cooling plate. The density-based topology optimization (TO) is an effective approach to resolving the growing thermal-hydraulic performance requirements of liquid cooling plate. However, existing TO methods can hardly optimize convective heat transfer directly which is the intrinsic heat transfer mechanism, due to the highly complex and evolving structural topologies, varying flow and temperature fields, making it extremely challenging to explicitly describe the heat transfer coefficient and heat transfer area during TO process. A convective heat transfer topology optimization (CTO) method is proposed in this study, where the iteratively evolving heat transfer coefficient is explicitly depicted by the field synergy theory in the thermal objective, and directly described by the velocity and temperature fields without relying on specific geometry. Combined with the explicit depiction of heat transfer area by the fractal geometry theory, a CTO framework is built for a direct optimization of convective heat transfer under both the laminar and turbulent flow conditions. The CTO tends to generate more hierarchical and directional structural topologies in optimization results, which is conducive to reducing low-velocity stagnation zones and improving flow direction in branched channels, achieving enhanced synergy and thermal-hydraulic performance in the optimized liquid cooling plates. Compared with the TO results without incorporation of field synergy theory, the CTO can reduce average temperature rise by 20% while improving the Nusselt number by 15% under laminar flow conditions, and reduce maximum temperature rise by 10.2% and pressure drop by 25% under turbulent flow conditions.

abstract: To supplement renewable energy sources and ensure energy security for consumer centers, the Brazilian power system relies on thermal power plants that remain on standby until the National System Operator (ONS) issues a dispatch request. This study considers a floating gas-fired thermal plant (powership) equipped with twelve 2 0 . 6 5 M W generator units. To meet the 30-minute dispatch tolerance, generator-driving engines must be maintained under pre-operational conditions, which is currently provided by a 1 . 6 2 M W resistive engine preheating system consuming up to 2 0 M W h / d a y . To improve energy efficiency, enhance the transient thermal response, and reduce the operating costs of the preheating system, this work proposes and evaluates three heat pump (HP)-based retrofit scenarios considering practical installation constraints of the powership, while assessing the photovoltaic (PV) generation potential of the available deck area as a complementary strategy. The application of HPs for this purpose has received little attention in the literature. The proposed configurations were evaluated through numerical simulations in MATLAB/Simulink and compared with the existing resistive system. The results show that the daily energy consumption of the engine preheating system was reduced by 7 0 . 4 - 8 0 . 0 % , and the time required to reach the engine standby temperature decreased from 2 ⁢ h ⁢ 5 1 ⁢ m i n to less than 1 ⁢ h ⁢ 0 3 ⁢ m i n , while energy balance and economic analyses indicated payback periods ranging from 3.2 to 8.1 years. The proposed retrofit scenarios demonstrate the feasibility of replacing M W -scale resistive engine preheating systems in thermal power plants with more energy-efficient HP-based systems, particularly when integrated with renewable energy sources.

From individual behaviour to collective benefit: the role of community agreements and demand flexibility in renewable energy communities
abstract: Renewable Energy Communities (RECs) play a vital role in advancing the transition toward sustainable energy systems; especially in Europe where they have been identified as a key tool towards decarbonization. However, a significant challenge to their success lies in ensuring sufficient member engagement. Currently, the legislative and financial schemes vary significantly by Country. Where available, the financial incentives provided often fail to offer adequate motivation, as community-level incentives do not always justify participation and, on the contrary, when available might hinder photovoltaic-owners from sharing their benefits. This study investigates how demand flexibility and heterogeneous access to investment affect REC performance, using the Italian regulatory and financial scheme as a case study. Four different operational scenarios are modelled using a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) approach implemented in Python and solved via Gurobi Optimizer, applied to the REC of Ventotene island. The first scenario assumes no demand flexibility, with members maintaining fixed consumption profiles. The second introduces differentiated demand response capabilities, where residential users are more flexible than commercial ones. The third and the fourth incorporates limited access to investment, allowing only a subset of members ("Prosumers") to install PV and storage systems, while others ("Consumers") contribute through high consumption flexibility. Results show that well-structured Community Agreements, by redistributing internal benefits and incentivizing adaptive behaviours, can significantly mobilise both Prosumers and Consumers. Increasing Consumers’ flexibility maximises shared renewable energy, improving the economic and environmental performance of the community even under constrained financial conditions.

Improving the temperature performance of district heating substations through two-stage thermal cascading: an assessment across different building typologies, climates and design solutions
abstract: Substations are fundamental components for the efficient operation of district heating networks. Cascaded layouts are widely recognized as effective solutions for enhancing substation temperature performance, thereby improving overall network efficiency. Despite their potential, clear and quantitative criteria for their design and operation remain lacking, particularly regarding their effectiveness in future low-temperature networks. Considering the renewed interest in district heating, this study investigates the thermal performance of a cascaded two-stage substation applied to two building typologies across six European climates. Using the average return temperature and the annual volume of water withdrawn from the network as key performance indicators, the results are compared with those of a conventional parallel layout. Results show that the cascaded configuration systematically reduces both the return temperature and the network water withdrawal, with benefits strongly dependent on climatic conditions and the relative share of space heating and domestic hot water in the building load. For the apartment building, reductions in the seasonal return temperature range from 0.9–1.2 °C in cold and continental climates to 4.7 °C in zones with milder winters. Corresponding reductions in annual water withdrawal range from 4.47% to 12.6%. For the office building, the reductions are smaller in cold climates (0.4–0.6 °C and 2.62% to 3.44%) due to the predominance of space heating demand over domestic hot water production. Sensitivity analyses on the size of the low-temperature heat exchanger for domestic hot water show that, in northern climates, performance improvements saturate once its heat transfer area becomes comparable to that of the high-temperature exchanger, with further enlargement yielding only marginal benefits below 1%. Conversely, substantially larger gains are achieved in southern regions. Under the assumption of a fixed total heat transfer area, allocating approximately 50% of this area to the low-temperature stage is identified as the most effective solution. Finally, the transition to lower operating temperatures leads to a slight reduction in the effectiveness of the two-stage configuration, with a more pronounced impact in mild climates. However, the two-stage configuration still outperforms the parallel layout.

Double-layer PCM plates integrated PV Trombe wall for climate-responsive power generation and thermal regulation
abstract: This study proposed a double-layer phase change material integrated photovoltaic Trombe wall (double-layer PV-PCMTW) for climate-responsive power generation and dynamic thermal regulation in buildings. The system responded to seasonal variations by coordinating switchable ventilation and double-layer PCM with distinct melting temperatures. A comprehensive transient simulation model was developed in TRNSYS to evaluate its annual performance in Wuhan, China. The proposed system was compared against a PV Trombe wall (PVTW) and a standalone PV system, assessing thermal, electrical, and carbon emission performance. The system effectively regulated indoor temperature fluctuations under natural conditions. On a typical summer day, its average indoor temperature was 0.30% lower than PVTW and 0.46% higher than the standalone PV system. On a typical winter day, it was 15.29% higher than PVTW and 25.88% higher than the standalone system. Compared to PVTW, the system reduced annual cooling and heating loads by 15.19% and 12.60%, respectively; relative to the standalone PV system, reductions reached 25.45% and 24.28%. Although the reduction in PV operating temperature was limited because of the finite latent heat capacity of the PCM, the proposed system achieved the highest annual electricity generation (1044.78 MJ) and annual carbon emission reduction (1986.97 kg CO₂), representing improvements of 23.10% over the PVTW. Economic analysis confirmed that the additional investment was offset by annual energy and environmental benefits, shortening the payback period versus the single-layer PCM system. The PV-PCMTW thus offers an effective strategy for improving building energy efficiency and long-term economic performance in hot-summer and cold-winter regions.

title: Impact of CO2 compensation scheme jointly with the European Union's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism: the case of Norway
abstract: Implementation of the European Union (EU)’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) potentially affects related sectors in Norway, particularly the aluminum production sector, the largest producer of primary aluminum in Europe and the largest aluminum supplier to the EU. Currently by a CO 2 compensation scheme, these affected sectors in Norway also receive financial compensation for additional electricity costs driven by higher carbon-intensive electricity generated in the EU under the regulation of the EU Emissions Trading System. This article studies how the Norwegian economy could be influenced by the CBAM and how the impact may be modified by the continuation of the CO 2 compensation scheme using a computable general equilibrium model tailored to the Norwegian economy. We show that proper CBAM implementation enhances the competitiveness of included industries in Norway. This is, however, insufficient to replace the effect of Norway’s CO 2 compensation scheme, particularly with the presence of market failures and regulatory issues like aluminum scrap loophole. Both policies have minimal macroeconomic and distributional effects, while contributing only modestly to global emission reductions.

abstract: The energy management of Hybrid Wheeled All-Terrain Vehicles (HWATVs) operating in unstructured environments faces significant challenges due to stochastic power demands and the lack of representative standard driving cycles. Existing strategies often fail to balance dynamic performance and fuel economy under such extreme conditions. This study proposes a systematic optimization framework integrating energy flow analysis with adaptive control. First, a high-fidelity powertrain test bench is established using the Design of Experiments (DOE) method to precisely quantify the multi-physical energy loss characteristics of the engine, motors, and battery. Subsequently, a driving cycle reconstruction method based on Principal Component Analysis (PCA), K-means clustering, and Markov chains is developed to extract four typical off-road patterns and synthesize stochastic validation cycles from real-vehicle data. On this basis, the Grey Wolf Optimizer (GWO) is employed to optimize mode-switching thresholds and battery State of Charge (SOC) maintenance ranges for each identified typical driving cycle. Incorporating these optimized parameter sets, an adaptive Energy Management Strategy (EMS) is established featuring online driving condition recognition to dynamically apply the optimal control logic. Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) validation under typical driving conditions and comprehensive driving cycles demonstrates that, compared to traditional rule-based strategies, the proposed approach exhibits superior robustness in stochastic environments. Specifically, it reduces fuel consumption by 0.99%–7.01% and decreases battery charge/discharge cycling frequency by 2.14%–15.30%. This research elucidates the energy-saving mechanism of coupling high-efficiency engine operation with minimized transmission path losses, providing a theoretical foundation for the efficient control of special vehicles in complex terrains.

Economic viability of low- and ultra-low-temperature district heating under varying demand and network conditions
abstract: District heating systems are considered key components of future sustainable heat supply, particularly in combination with heat pumps and renewable energy sources. However, their economic viability strongly depends on local boundary conditions, demand characteristics, and system design. This study investigates the economic performance of low-temperature district heating (LTDH) and ultra-low-temperature district heating (ULTDH) in comparison with decentralized heat supply solutions based on heat pumps, using a case study in northern Germany. Three main scenario groups were defined, modeled and simulated to investigate the influence of: (i) building renovation leading to reduced heat demand and linear heat density, (ii) proportional scaling of connected heat demand at constant network length, and (iii) expansion of the district heating network scale. Key influencing factors such as heat demand density, system temperature levels, and the share of high-temperature demand are systematically analyzed. The results show that linear heat density and temperature-related parameters are the dominant drivers of economic viability for centralized heat supply systems. Under the investigated case-study conditions and cost assumptions, LTDH is economically competitive across most of the analyzed scenarios. However, this advantage decreases in areas with very low connected heat demand density, where decentralized heat pump solutions become preferable. The viability of ULTDH is strongly constrained by the achievable reduction of high-temperature demand and by the cost and performance of building-side booster heat pumps. The findings highlight the importance of coordinated, stepwise planning strategies that jointly consider building renovation, heating system temperature reduction, network development, and local heat-source availability. Such integrated approaches are essential to assess the long-term economic viability of low-temperature district heating systems.

abstract: High-temperature heat pumps (HTHPs) are recognized as a key technology for industrial decarbonization. However, their effective deployment and integration with low-temperature district heating networks require operating conditions that balance energy performance and economic competitiveness. This study investigates the optimal operation of a moderate HTHP using R-450A through a multi-objective optimization framework based on experimental data. Grey-box regression models were developed from measurements collected on an experimental prototype and used to predict the coefficient of performance, pressure ratio, and heating capacity as functions of evaporation temperature, condensation temperature, and compressor frequency. The models were integrated into a genetic algorithm to simultaneously maximize performance and minimize operating cost. The optimization was performed for four heat supply temperatures (70, 80, 90, and 100 °C) and considering electricity and district heating market conditions in eight European countries. The results show that increasing the condensation temperature reduces system performance, with the maximum performance decreasing from approximately 5.0 at 70 °C to 3.0 at 100 °C. The optimal operating conditions consistently correspond to the minimum compressor frequency, while the evaporation temperature depends on the trade-off between thermodynamic and economic objectives. Energy and environmental assessments demonstrate that optimal-compromise solutions provide substantially greater primary energy savings and avoided carbon dioxide emissions than minimum-cost solutions. The findings highlight the importance of multi-objective optimization for maximizing the contribution of HTHPs to industrial decarbonization and sector coupling applications.

Multi-criteria assessment of solid oxide fuel cells: Experimental, life cycle, and techno-economic perspectives
abstract: Solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs) are widely recognized as a promising technology for energy conversion in the transition toward a net-zero future. However, existing studies often evaluate experimental performance, environmental impacts, and economic feasibility in isolation. In addition, life cycle assessments (LCAs) rely heavily on secondary data and literature-based performance parameters that may not accurately represent real-world fabrication and operational conditions. To address these limitations, a comprehensive multi-criteria evaluation framework was developed in which experimental investigation, LCA, and techno-economic analysis (TEA) were integrated within a unified and empirically grounded approach for anode-supported SOFCs. The LCA was performed using three methodologies (CML, ReCiPe, and EF), and the results indicated that the Crofer 22 APU interconnect was the dominant contributor to the global warming and acidification potentials during the fabrication stage. In contrast, during the operational phase, environmental performance was primarily governed by hydrogen carbon intensity, with the baseline (stack-level) carbon intensity of SOFC electricity (0.017 kgCO 2 /kWh) increasing by 0.05 kgCO 2 /kWh for every 1 kgCO 2 /kgH 2 increase in hydrogen carbon intensity. For the province of Alberta, it was found that hydrogen carbon intensities exceeding 3.5 kgCO 2 /kgH 2 reverse the net sustainability benefits of SOFC-based systems. Economically, when the hydrogen price is increased from $1/kg to $5/kg, the monthly operating cost of residential systems to supporting combined heat and power increases from $244 to $974.

System design and comprehensive analysis of compressed air energy storage assisted flexible operation of solar power plants
abstract: To effectively improve the energy utilization and operational flexibility of solar power generation, this study proposes an integrated system that couples CAES with a solar thermal power plant and a photovoltaic power station. In charging process, excess PV power drives the compressor and low-temp condensed water from solar thermal regeneration cools outlet hot compressed air to recycle compression heat. In discharging, process, graded solar thermal feedwater preheats released compressed air. Through system integration, the compression heat is effectively utilized, while the thermal energy storage equipment originally required in conventional CAES systems is reduced. A thermodynamic model of the proposed integrated system is established, and energy, exergy, and economic analyses are conducted to evaluate system performance. The analysis results indicate that the CAES subsystem achieves a round-trip efficiency of 73.50%, an exergy efficiency of 80.97%, and an energy storage density of 11.35 MJ/m³. The overall efficiency of the integrated system reaches 27.70%, and the peak-shaving depth is 4.71% during the day and 10.30% at night. Furthermore, the dynamic payback period of the system is 4.34 years, and the net present value is 6247.63 k$. This study provides a feasible technical solution for improving the operational flexibility of solar power generation.

Load transfer mechanisms and degradation hotspots in floating vertical-axis wind turbines under coupled aero-hydro-elastic-mooring effects
abstract: The coupled aerodynamic mechanisms and structural nonlinearities of floating vertical-axis wind turbines (VAWTs) under multi-scale loading present significant challenges for efficient and reliable numerical prediction. To address these challenges, this study develops a hybrid-fidelity fluid-structure interaction (FSI) framework by integrating computational fluid dynamics (CFD), the finite element method (FEM), potential-flow theory, and the Morison equation. The proposed framework is used to investigate the coupled aero–elastic–hydro responses of both rigid and flexible models under combined wind-wave excitation. Results show that rotor flexibility can convert part of the aerodynamic loading into structural strain energy, thereby attenuating the transmission of aerodynamic overturning moments and lateral asymmetric loads to the platform. However, blade deformation modifies the local effective angle of attack and tangential force distribution, resulting in a 7.85% lower mean power coefficient compared with the rigid model. The smaller lateral motions and load fluctuations of the flexible model suppress wake mixing, making the velocity-deficit region more persistent. The mooring system shows stress concentration near the fairlead and periodic lift-off/recontact near the touchdown point. In addition, pronounced stress concentration occurs in the internal shear web near the blade–strut connection, where spanwise shear forces and combined bending–torsional moments lead to the maximum von Mises stress of 6.354 × 10 8 Pa. Overall, these results demonstrate the importance of incorporating rotor flexibility in coupled response prediction and provide guidance for refined aerodynamic, structural, and mooring design of large-scale floating VAWTs.

Experimental investigation of propane/pentane (R290/R601) mixtures in a residential high-temperature heat pump: effects of mixture composition and internal heat exchanger
abstract: Decarbonizing the building sector requires heat pumps to be increasingly retrofitted into existing residential buildings, where conventional hydronic systems often demand high supply temperatures. Propane is a promising low global warming refrigerant for this purpose, but its operation can be limited by high compressor discharge temperatures under severe conditions. This work experimentally investigates whether blending propane with pentane can mitigate this limitation and how a bypassable internal heat exchanger affects system performance. A heat pump prototype was built and tested with pure propane and 90/10 and 80/20 wt.% propane/pentane mixtures under space heating and domestic hot water conditions, with and without the internal heat exchanger. The results show that no single configuration was optimal over the whole operating envelope. When sufficient margin on the compressor discharge temperature was available, the IHX improved the COP by up to 49% compared to the non-IHX cases. Increasing the pentane content reduced the compressor discharge temperature by up to 18 K compared to pure propane, increasing the thermal operating margin, but also requiring higher compressor speeds to deliver the same heating capacity. When all refrigerants reached the target heating capacity, pentane addition produced small and non-systematic COP variations in space heating, whereas improvements of up to 7% were observed in domestic hot water conditions. Overall, propane–pentane mixtures and IHX operation provided complementary means of improving efficiency and extending the operating envelope, highlighting their potential for residential high-temperature heat pump applications.

abstract: This study evaluates the techno-economic performance of integrating a carbon capture and utilisation (CCU) power-to-methanol pathway into a Danish Waste-to-Energy (WtE) plant within a local energy system context. Using a dynamic hourly model based on a real-world case (Thisted Varmeforsyning), the analysis captures the interaction between electricity price variability, carbon capture, grid-connected electrolysis, methanol synthesis, storage systems, and district heating operation. The results showed that the levelised cost of methanol (LCOMeOH) remains high, ≈ 1,288 €/t, and is dominated by hydrogen production, with electrolyser electricity consumption accounting for 60% of total costs. Sensitivity analysis revealed that system economics are highly dependent on electricity-related conditions: a 50% change in electricity prices changes LCOMeOH by 21%, while full tariff exemption reduces costs by 17%. In contrast, even substantial direct subsidies, modelled as financial credit per tonne of utilised CO 2 , have a limited impact (<4%). Integrating CCU with WtE fundamentally alters the plant from a modest net electricity exporter (+13,285 MWh/a) to a major grid consumer (-419,732 MWh/a), while simultaneously becoming a key heat supplier, displacing over 70% of heat purchases from other units. Overall, the study highlights that the viability of WtE-based power-to-methanol depends primarily on access to low-cost electricity as well as favourable regulatory conditions, and requires evaluation within an integrated energy system framework rather than at the process level alone.

Physics-aware deep reinforcement learning for radiant floor heating: A Sim-to-Real framework for proactive energy management
abstract: Radiant floor heating systems present significant thermodynamic control challenges due to their massive thermal inertia, often causing traditional reactive controllers to fail to balance energy efficiency with occupant thermal comfort. This study proposes a physics-aware Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) framework for residential energy management that exploits the building's concrete slab as short-term thermal energy storage. To establish the simulation-to-reality (Sim-to-Real) framework, a reliable 5R3C thermal network model was developed and calibrated via a gradient-based optimization approach. The proposed Deep Q-Network (DQN) agent uses engineered thermodynamic state features, notably indoor temperature gradients and predictive look-ahead horizons, enabling the agent to characterize the thermal mass and execute proactive load-shifting strategies. Furthermore, to accommodate dynamic operational schedules, the framework integrates a lighting-based heuristic proxy for the autonomous generation of adaptive target glidepaths, allowing the agent to execute pre-heating and thermal coasting. Optimized via the Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) algorithm, the physics-aware DRL policy demonstrated exceptional robustness in a real-world deployment. Results show that the proposed framework achieves significant energy savings ranging from 9.7% to 14.4% in simulation and 15.9% during real-world online control compared to the conventional bang-bang baseline, while satisfying dynamic thermal comfort constraints with negligible thermal violations. This research provides a scalable and cost-effective Sim-to-Real solution for next-generation building energy management systems, proving that high-inertia residential heating can be optimized as virtual thermal batteries without requiring computationally intensive online optimization.

Nanoporous molecular springs as energy-density extenders for liquid-piston compressed air energy storage: A performance and techno-economic assessment
abstract: High-pressure liquid-piston compressed-air energy storage (LP-CAES) is mechanically simple and scalable, yet its value is limited by footprint-constrained energy density and utilization-dependent economics. This study evaluates an LP-CAES configuration augmented with zeolitic imidazolate framework (ZIF-8) molecular springs (MS), where pressure-driven water intrusion/extrusion into hydrophobic nanopores introduces an auxiliary work-storage pathway and modifies the gas-liquid volume dynamics during charge and discharge. A cycle-resolved lumped 0-D model couples real-gas thermodynamics, hydraulic pressure/flow losses, and physics-based component representations for a positive-displacement pump/motor set, Pelton turbine, and induction generator. For a 70–300 bar operating cycle, ZIF-8 integration, with a 2:1 dilution, increases the stored energy density by 32%. On a per-cycle basis, delivered electricity increases by 26.3%, while charging electricity rises by 30.5%, resulting in a reduction in roundtrip efficiency (RTE) from 55.7% to 53.9%. The MS channel exhibits 69.1% work recovery, with a net MS loss of 0.522 kWh per cycle, indicating that MS primarily acts as a capacity and energy-density extender rather than an intrinsic RTE enhancer. When scaled to a plant delivering 40 MWh per cycle, the baseline MS case reduces capital expenditure (CAPEX) by 16.3% and lowers the levelized cost of energy storage (LCOES) by 1.7% at daily cycling, while maintaining higher net present value (NPV) across three utilization scenarios, although the broader economic advantage remains scenario-dependent. These results suggest that ZIF-8 integration should be viewed as a vessel-level capacity extender, most attractive where storage footprint is constrained or additional charge acceptance can monetize curtailed or low-price electricity.

A simulation-guided roadmap to efficient ethanol production via carbon monoxide electrolysis
abstract: Electrochemical ethanol production via carbon monoxide reduction reaction (CORR) offers a promising alternative to conventional routes, but practical implementation requires improvements in selectivity, current density, and single-pass conversion efficiency (SPCE). Here, we couple insights from multi-physics modeling and techno-economic analysis for CORR-to-ethanol in scalable membrane electrode assembly (MEA) electrolyzers, with the aim of identifying pathways to match today’s ethanol price. The model resolves the local reaction environment, voltage-loss distribution, and system performance under various operating, structural, transport, and kinetic parameters. A one-factor-at-a-time sensitivity analysis is performed to identify the parameters that strongly affect the ethanol partial current density, followed by Taguchi optimization to determine favorable parameter combinations. Scenario analysis reveals that kinetics-related parameters primarily govern ethanol selectivity while kinetic and system improvements contribute to current density and SPCE. The ideal-performance case electrolyzer configuration and operation conditions enable a full-cell ethanol energy efficiency (EE) of 57.3% (1.83 V) and an ethanol SPCE of 89.1% at a current density of 704 mA cm -2 . This performance corresponds to an ethanol electroproduction cost of 1,594 $ ton -1 , approximately 47% lower than literature benchmarks.

Comparative techno-economic-environmental investigation of hybrid renewable energy systems for combined cooling, heating and power provision to hotel buildings in hot desert climates
abstract: Hybrid renewable energy systems (HRESs) are suitable for addressing the intermittency of separate, individual renewable resources, and for more reliable and flexible energy provision. They are thus expected to play a vital role in promoting the wider use of renewable energy technologies, which are a core element of energy transition pathways. In this study, various combinations of renewable energy technologies and product options are investigated within selected HRES configurations. These include photovoltaic (PV) panels, solar thermal collectors (STCs), PV-thermal (PV-T) collectors, wind turbines (WTs) and biomass boilers (BBs), representing a range of technical performance and cost levels. Detailed techno-economic-environmental assessments of these HRESs are performed for a case study of a hotel in Fayoum, Egypt, given the growing importance of the local tourism sector. Sensitivity analysis of solar field area and number of WTs are performed, along with optimisation based on net present cost (NPC) to determine optimal systems for power, heating and cooling provision to the selected hotel. The results show that PV panels, especially the low-cost product options, enable the HRESs to deliver favourable economic performance, with a lowest NPC of $195.7k, along with a corresponding levelised cost of energy (LCOE) of 0.060 $/kWh, a payback period (PBP) of 6.3 years and annual carbon emissions (ACE) of 22.1 ton/year. The PV-T-based systems are also promising, as they achieve the highest levels of self-sufficiency ratio (up to ∼40%), while having a significant potential for further technical improvements as well as cost reductions are expected in the future. From an environmental perspective, the PV- and PV-T-based systems are similar, delivering significant emissions reductions (>50%). A modified HRES layout that splits the heat provision into hot water and space heating satisfied by renewables (solar and biomass) and the hotel’s existing air-conditioning system is also proposed. A decrease of 10% in NPC relative to the original PV-based HRES is achieved, while the LCOE decreases from 0.060 to 0.054 $/kWh and the PBP from 6.3 to 3.4 years. The modified HRES layout benefits from a smaller boiler, lower biomass consumption and less electricity fed/sold to the grid. The results and conclusions from this study can provide valuable guidance for the design and establishment of HRESs in practical applications, especially for the selection of available renewable energy technologies and product options, thus facilitating the wider deployment of such promising systems.

The role of thermal energy storage in enhancing the robustness of solar-thermal-driven polygeneration systems for a dairy industry
abstract: Solar thermal-driven polygeneration (STDP) systems represent a promising approach to the production of clean and efficient energy for agri-food industries, with a wide range of temperatures for heating, cooling and power applications. This study conducted a technical, economic, and environmental assessment with particular focus on the role of three different thermal energy storage (TES) systems on the performance of STDP systems consisting of parabolic trough solar collectors, cogeneration Organic Rankine Cycle, auxiliary boiler, and mechanical chiller, to supply heating, cooling, and electricity services to a dairy industry located in Tauste, Spain. The analysis was carried out using a mixed-integer linear programming model that optimizes the selection and sizing of the equipment, as well as its operational performance over a full typical year. In order to evaluate the performance of the proposed system, 833 distinct optimisation cases were solved to study: (i) the role of TES systems located at different points (and corresponding temperature levels) within the plant layout; (ii) the interaction of the proposed system with the power grid; and (iii) sensitivity and robustness analyses based on variations in energy prices. The results showed that the proposed system achieved an annual solar fraction of 37.2%, with slightly lower costs (about 5%) and lower greenhouse gas emissions (about 37%) compared to the conventional supply system. In addition, the relative contribution of the different TES systems was determined, as well as the positive interaction with the power grid, which acted as a “virtual” energy storage system, in improving system performance.

Defossilisation options for non-road mobile machinery in mining and forestry
abstract: The non-road mobile machinery (NRMM) sector is an increasingly significant contributor to greenhouse gas emissions due to its high energy intensity and reliance on fossil fuel-based operations. NRMM include a diverse set of segments and machinery types, many of which operate in harsh environments for extended periods. This study assesses the potential for the defossilisation of two representative NRMM segments, mining and forestry, by analysing on-site renewable electricity supply for a mining site and the use of battery-electric forwarders in forestry supported by mobile battery containers. The results demonstrate that full or near-full defossilisation for both segments is technically feasible, although optimal solutions are region-dependent. Solar-dominant regions, such as northern Chile, require a combination of solar photovoltaics and high battery storage (4.0 MWh cap /MW p ), to meet mining energy demand. Conversely, wind-dominant and hybrid solar PV-wind regions can minimise storage requirements by 7-26 times for the same annual electricity demand, partially relying on green e-diesel generators for balancing. For forestry applications, frequent relocation limits the practicality of on-site renewable electricity generation. However, combining battery-electric forwarders with mobile battery containers offers a viable pathway, with annualised system costs declining by 12-13% in 2030-2050. While initially capital-intensive, by 2050 this option is only 2.0% higher in cost than baseline fossil fuel-powered machinery. The transition to green e-fuels proves even more competitive, yielding 4.5% lower costs compared to the baseline in 2050. Despite limited adoption of renewable energy and electrification in the sector, tightening emission regulations and CO 2 pricing may accelerate this transition.

Scheduling heat loads among multiple units in a combined heat and power plant for greater operational flexibility: Fundamentals and economic benefits
abstract: Combined heat and power (CHP) can enhance energy efficiency but restrict the operational flexibility of thermal power plants. As multiple CHP units make up a CHP plant and vary in energy efficiency and operational flexibility, reasonable scheduling of heat loads among multiple CHP units may maximize the benefits of the CHP plant. In this study, a novel heat scheduling method was proposed to enhance the overall operational flexibility of power plants. Fundamentals for the proposed idea, including the operational domain, energy efficiency, and exergy efficiency of multiple CHP units, are studied. The results indicate that: The reference CHP plant contains two EC (extraction condensing) units and two EBP (extraction back pressure) units, and these two types of units exhibit different heat-power coupling characteristics, energy efficiency, and exergy efficiency. Using the optimal allocation method proposed in this study, the peak shaving capacity ratio of the CHP plant can be increased by a maximum of 13.84% compared to the average allocation. Besides, to measure the operating economy, a critical coal-electricity price ratio (CCEPR) is proposed, which has an economic advantage when the coal-electricity price ratio is lower than CCEPR. For optimal scheduling of heat loads on a typical day, the minimum CCEPR values occur at 23:00 and 24:00, with values of 4.70 CNY·t -1 /CNY·(MW·h) -1 and 4.72 CNY·t -1 /CNY·(MW·h) -1 . The total operating economic benefits of the optimal allocation method have significant advantages compared to average allocation. The corresponding daily operating income difference is negatively correlated with coal prices and positively correlated with electricity prices. Taking the coal price of 1000 CNY·t -1 and the valley electricity price of 200 CNY·(MW·h) -1 as examples, optimal allocation can increase the total operating income of the CHP plant by 891.6 thousand CNY per day.

Research on the implementation path of industrial carbon reduction in Inner Mongolia from a system perspective
abstract: In 2022, China's industrial sector accounted for 77% of the country's total carbon emissions. As a key energy strategic base, Inner Mongolia faces significant decarbonization challenges while ensuring energy supply. To achieve the dual goals of economic growth and emission reduction, a scientific industrial emission reduction strategy is urgently needed. This study employs the Energy Policy Simulator (EPS) model combined with System Dynamics (SD) and Monte Carlo simulation techniques to build a scenario model for Inner Mongolia’s industrial sector, based on historical data from 2016 to 2022. Various scenarios of Industrial Management and Efficiency Enhancement (IMEE) and carbon pricing are analyzed, with consideration of uncertainties in the energy restructuring process. Results show that: (1) Monte Carlo breakpoint tests indicate a coal consumption share of approximately 45-50% serves as a structural pivot to weaken carbon lock-in, rather than a precise deterministic cutoff; (2) Although carbon pricing induces the first local emissions peak, 39.0% of Monte Carlo trajectories exhibit emissions rebound, defined as 2060 emissions exceeding the first local peak (95% exact binomial CI: 34.7%-43.4%). The combined IMEE and carbon pricing scenario yields lower median emissions in 2060, a narrower 95% uncertainty interval, and reduced rebound risk, effectively hedging energy structure fluctuations. Compared with the baseline, the composite scenario reduces emissions by 1.32-1.54 Gt in 2060, with cumulative reductions of 39.8-46.8 Gt over 2024-2060.

A comparison of Mixed-Integer Linear Programming and Genetic Algorithm–Linear Programming to optimize a non-interconnected island energy system
abstract: This study compares a Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulation with a hybrid Genetic Algorithm–Linear Programming (GA–LP) framework for the joint optimization of technology sizing and hourly operation in the non-interconnected multi-energy system of Favignana, Italy. Both approaches use the same technology portfolio, twelve monthly representative days, techno-economic assumptions, and performance indicators. The MILP jointly optimizes technology capacities and operational variables within a single mixed-integer linear problem. The GA–LP framework instead decomposes planning and operation: the upper-level Genetic Algorithm explores the technology-design space, while a lower-level LP determines the optimal hourly dispatch for each fixed candidate design. This structure allows the exploration of a nonlinear design–performance relationship while excluding hourly dispatch variables from the evolutionary search, thereby reducing its dimensionality.Both formulations substantially improve the reference system in terms of annualized cost, primary energy consumption, and life-cycle CO 2 -equivalent emissions. MILP reduces annualized cost by approximately 55%–60% and CO 2 -equivalent emissions by approximately 65%–80%, depending on the objective. GA–LP achieves annualized-cost reductions of up to 70%, while emission reductions exceed 90% under environmental optimization. The two formulations produce different sizing and dispatch patterns because they adopt distinct planning–operation couplings and storage-operation constraints. MILP requires approximately 9 s per objective function, whereas GA–LP requires approximately 185–189 s. Overall, hybrid decomposition offers a flexible and computationally manageable option for complex island multi-energy planning.

A time-series clustering framework for sector-coupled capacity expansion models
abstract: The growing importance of hydrogen and sector coupling increases the complexity of Capacity Expansion Models (CEMs) and underscores the need for time-series aggregation methods that balance accuracy with computational efficiency. While previous studies have focused on developing methods for small-scale power sector CEM, this work compares three traditional clustering approaches with a novel DTW-based method (DTW-VD) in terms of statistical accuracy and applies them in a single-node and a multi-node sector-coupled CEMs with seasonal storage. DTW-VD achieves the highest statistical accuracy and best approximates the full-resolution objective function in the single-node case for up to 125 representative days. In the multi-node model, where the true solution is not available, investment decisions based on DTW-VD achieve the best operational performance in 2050. Overall, using two different models and three different weather years, the findings indicate that the performance of time-series aggregation methods depends on the characteristics of the optimization problem, the underlying dataset, and the chosen temporal resolution. The proposed method performs particularly well in complex systems and when a low number of representative periods is used.

title: Configuration selection and lunar daytime off-design evaluation of power generation-refrigeration coupled systems for lunar bases
abstract: Efficient and reliable combined cooling and power systems are essential for long-duration lunar bases, where radiative heat rejection is strongly affected by the wide variation of the equivalent heat-sink temperature (Ts) during the lunar daytime. In this study, seven coupled power generation-cooling system models are developed. A unified multi-indicator evaluation framework and working fluid screening strategy are established to compare the system performance under a common lunar boundary. Under the baseline condition of Ts = 100 K, the Organic Rankine Cycle (ORC)–vapor compression refrigeration (VCR) system achieves the highest energy utilization factor (EUF) of 73.2% and coefficient of performance (COP) of 6.30, and the ORC-ejector refrigeration cycle (ERC) system has the simplest structure and the highest net output power, while the transcritical CO2 Rankine cycle (tRC)–VCR system achieves the highest exergy efficiency of 56.5%. Based on thermodynamic and compactness performance, these three coupled systems are selected for further evaluation. Quasi-steady off-design analysis over the 90–325 K lunar-daytime Ts range shows that tRC-VCR system has the best robustness, which is attributed to active dual-pressure regulation in the tRC–VCR system.

title: Modulation of thermal properties by Al2O3 nanoparticle in LiCl-KCl molten salt: Experimental and molecular dynamics simulation study
Fluctuating industrial waste heat sources for power generation by Organic Rankine Cycles: Assessing the integration of a thermal energy storage system and potential operational strategies
abstract: Industrial waste heat recovery (WHR) using Organic Rankine Cycle (ORC) systems offers significant potential for enhanced energy efficiency in energy-intensive sectors. However, highly fluctuating heat source conditions result in off-design operation, causing efficiency losses, increased mechanical stress and repeated shutdown events. Integrating thermal energy storage (TES) can mitigate these effects, yet its performance strongly depends on the applied operating strategy and dynamic system behaviour. This study investigates the operation of a 2 MWel industrial WHR-ORC system with an integrated packed-bed TES using real plant measurement data. Three storage control strategies (minimum-load prioritisation, nominal-load harvesting and ramp-rate smoothing) are evaluated using a two-staged simulation framework consisting of long-term quasi-stationary modelling and detailed dynamic process simulation. The approach enables the evaluation of energy utilisation and operational stability under realistic transient boundary conditions. Results show that TES integration significantly improves system operation compared to the baseline without storage. The stability-oriented strategy reduces shutdown events from 1645 to 30 and decreases downtime by 41%, while maintaining a slight efficiency increase. The harvesting-oriented strategy achieves the highest energy utilisation with a relative increase of 6%, but with more start-stop events. The ramp-rate strategy provides balanced operation with strongly reduced mechanical stress but slightly reduced energy recovery. The findings demonstrate that storage operation strategy is as decisive as TES size for real industrial applications. The presented methodology provides a framework for designing and controlling TES-assisted ORC systems and supports future techno-economic optimisation of industrial waste heat recovery plants.

Time-resolved advanced exergy analysis of a field-validated solar–hydrogen microgrid with anion-exchange-membrane electrolysis and detailed balance-of-plant modelling
abstract: Stand-alone solar–hydrogen microgrids offer a promising solution for long-duration renewable energy storage, yet identifying the sources and improvement potential of thermodynamic inefficiencies in such integrated systems remains challenging under realistic operating conditions. This study presents a time-resolved advanced exergy analysis based on a validated TRNSYS (Transient System Simulation Tool) model of the stand-alone hydrogen microgrid of the Charles Darwin University (CDU) Renewable Energy Microgrid Hub for Applied Research and Training (REMHART) in Darwin, incorporating photovoltaic generation, four pressurised anion-exchange-membrane (AEM) electrolysers, hydrogen storage, and a 5-kW proton-exchange-membrane fuel cell (PEMFC). A supervisory controller dynamically coordinates hydrogen production, storage, and dispatch. Each electrochemical component is represented by a physics-based voltage–current formulation calibrated with field measurements to capture realistic electrochemical and auxiliary losses. The model explicitly accounts for balance-of-plant subsystems, including a deionised reverse-osmosis water unit, dryers, valves, cooling fans, and other auxiliary components whose exergetic effects are commonly neglected. A TRNSYS-based simulation framework is coupled with advanced exergy decomposition to separate exergy destruction into endogenous and exogenous as well as avoidable and unavoidable components over time. Results show that the supervisory control effectively dampens component interactions, leading to near-zero exogenous destruction, while the PEMFC exhibits the highest fractional avoidability. The PEM fuel cell, balance-of-plant and AEM electrolyser exhibit avoidabilities of approximately 32%, 19% and 9%, respectively. At the system level, the time-averaged avoidable exergy destruction is approximately 15%, indicating that future efficiency improvements are achievable but should primarily focus on component-level technological improvements such as stack enhancement and auxiliary optimisation.

Optimization storage pressure for pumped hydro compressed air energy storage considering water-air vessel thermodynamics
abstract: The increasing penetration of renewable energy has created a growing need for large-scale, high-efficiency energy storage. Pumped hydro compressed air energy storage (PH-CAES) uses natural elevation differences to form an approximately isobaric water-air vessel, providing a promising solution for large-scale physical energy storage. In conventional preliminary designs, however, the storage pressure is often determined directly from the maximum available water head. This practice may force the system to operate at unnecessarily high pressure, causing substantial exergy destruction in heat exchangers and reducing round-trip efficiency. To address this issue, this paper develops a thermodynamic model of the isobaric water-air vessel and clarifies its near-isothermal air storage characteristics. On this basis, an optimization framework is established to determine the storage pressure together with the compression and expansion ratios under realistic equipment constraints. The proposed design method is applied to a planned 50 MW PH-CAES plant in eastern China and compared with conventional designs based on full water-head utilization and equal compression ratios. The optimized design improves the round-trip efficiency from 69.81\% to 71.56\%, confirming the importance of determining storage pressure based on thermodynamic matching rather than maximum water-head utilization alone. The results further reveal a rise-decline relationship between optimal round-trip efficiency and storage pressure, confirming the existence of an optimal pressure under given equipment constraints. Sensitivity analysis identifies the isentropic efficiencies of the compressor and expander as the dominant factors affecting round-trip efficiency, whereas the optimal storage pressure is primarily governed by the maximum heat storage temperature and compressor isentropic efficiency.

Synergistic heat and illumination management in phase change material assisted spectral-splitting photovoltaic/thermal collector design
abstract: Concentrated photovoltaic/thermal (CPV/T) systems remain limited by incomplete spectral control and inadequate thermal decoupling between the photovoltaic cell and the thermal absorber, while most existing models do not fully resolve phase change material (PCM) optical transitions or compare receiver designs under consistent conditions. To address these gaps, this study develops and validates a three-dimensional transient multiphysics CFD model of a CPV/T receiver incorporating a hybrid spectral filter composed of a selective liquid filter (water or propylene glycol) and a PCM layer (RT25 or S27). The model incorporates non-gray radiation and temperature- and phase-dependent optical properties to accurately capture the transient coupling of optical, thermal, and electrical processes during PCM melting. Parametric analyses are conducted to assess the effects of SLF/PCM material selection, Reynolds number, concentration ratio, seasonal boundary conditions, filter thickness, and alternative receiver topologies on system performance. Results show that accurately accounting for PCM optical evolution is essential for realistic prediction of spectral beam splitting and system transients. Propylene glycol accelerates PCM melting and enhances gross thermal recovery, while water provides stronger infrared shielding and negligible pumping penalty; PW-S27 at higher Re is recommended for practical operation, reaching about 48.3% net efficiency. Increasing CR from 10 to 40 improves PCM activation and energy yield while the air-gap-assisted design limits PV temperature rise. Topology analysis confirms that the proposed hybrid filter above the PV cell provides the best durability-oriented performance, reducing degradation acceleration factor by 5.69 compared with the filterless case while maintaining high useful heat recovery. This work provides design guidance for durable, high-flux CPV/T spectral filters.

Optimizing hybrid SMR–renewable energy systems for remote and climate-vulnerable communities: A techno-economic framework
abstract: Remote and climate-vulnerable northern communities in Canada remain heavily dependent on diesel-based electricity and heating, leading to high energy costs, fuel-supply challenges, and significant greenhouse gas emissions. This study develops a techno-economic framework to evaluate hybrid small modular reactor (SMR)-renewable energy systems for remote regions. The framework integrates a 6 MW light-water SMR, wind and photovoltaic (PV) generation, battery energy storage, combined heat and power (CHP) recovery, and hydrogen production from surplus electricity. A representative cluster of northern Canadian communities is used as a case study, and two hybrid system configurations are assessed. The SMR-wind-battery configuration achieves the best economic performance, with a levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) of $0.26/kWh and a net present cost (NPC) of $241 million, compared with $0.31/kWh and $288 million for the SMR-wind-PV-battery configuration. A diesel-only reference system yields an LCOE of $0.72/kWh and an NPC of $675 million. In both optimized configurations, the SMR supplies 52.5 GWh/year of electricity, representing 75-78% of total generation, and provides about 96 GWh th /year of recoverable thermal energy through CHP operation. Surplus electricity supports hydrogen production of approximately 215,000-261,000 kg/year. Sensitivity and Monte Carlo analyses identify SMR capital cost as the dominant source of economic uncertainty, followed by battery and wind-turbine costs. A key contribution of this study is the development of an integrated framework for assessing SMR-centered hybrid energy systems in remote and climate-vulnerable communities. The results demonstrate the potential of SMR-centered hybrid energy systems to provide reliable, low-carbon, and economically competitive energy for remote and off-grid regions.

Cross-building reinforcement learning for zero-shot HVAC control in residential buildings
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has shown promise for residential Heating, Ventilation, and Air Conditioning (HVAC) control, but conventional approaches require target-building data, model construction, and policy training, limiting scalability in newly constructed houses. Although transfer learning reduces this burden, scalable zero-shot RL control that avoids target-building data collection, model calibration, and policy retraining remains insufficiently investigated. This study therefore has two objectives: (1) to develop a Cross-building Trust Region Policy Optimization (TRPO) framework for zero-shot residential air-conditioning control, and (2) to determine whether it can achieve performance comparable to room-specific RL in unseen rooms without retraining. EnergyPlus generated residential rooms with diverse thermal characteristics, and thermal-performance indicators were incorporated into the state space to condition the policy on room-specific responses. A single TRPO policy was trained across these tasks and tested in resistance-capacitance (RC) simulation environments constructed from data for two unseen target rooms; these data were used only for evaluation. For the small-design-load room, Cross-building TRPO reduced energy consumption to 64.57% of the fixed-setpoint baseline while maintaining a 100% comfort ratio. For the large-design-load room, where the baseline operated at a high coefficient of performance (COP), both room-specific TRPO and Cross-building TRPO yielded limited additional improvement. Overall, Cross-building TRPO achieved performance close to room-specific TRPO without target-room retraining, demonstrating the feasibility of building-performance-conditioned zero-shot HVAC control. In practice, pre-trained HVAC controllers could be deployed in newly constructed residential buildings using available thermal-performance information, reducing on-site data collection and policy retraining requirements and supporting large-scale deployment.

Physics-informed design of PV coupled alkaline water electrolysis with battery energy storage under fluctuating power through dynamic modeling
abstract: Expanding renewable energy is essential for sustainability, but fluctuating power sources pose significant challenges to the stability of green hydrogen systems. Although PV coupled water electrolyzer systems are often designed using conventional techno-economic metrics, such approaches neglect dynamic electrochemical and thermal responses under variable power operation. This study develops a physics-based dynamic model for a PV coupled alkaline water electrolysis and battery system. The model resolves coupled dynamics across the stack and the balance of plant. Twelve scenarios are proposed to examine the impact of physically informed considerations on system design. Each scenario is evaluated using three decision-making methods, comparing a conventional indicator set with an augmented set that includes physically informed indicators. The conventional indicators include LCOH, curtailment, and battery state of charge variation, while the physically informed indicators include cell voltage variation, rapid O 2 in H 2 rise duration, and system efficiency. The results show that the Const 695 kW scenario held rank 3 in all three methods under the conventional indicator set but fell below rank 10 when the physically informed indicators were included, revealing safety risks that conventional indicators failed to capture. In contrast, the Ramp 695 kW scenario ranked first across all evaluation cases, confirming that a large AWE with a small battery operated to follow the PV output is robust under both economic and safety perspectives. These findings demonstrate that physics-based dynamic modeling is essential for identifying hidden safety vulnerabilities and enabling more informed design decisions under fluctuating renewable power.

abstract: With increasing awareness of sustainable manufacturing, there has been growing research on energy-efficient flexible job shop scheduling problems. However, obtaining highly energy-efficient schedules remains challenging because the problem is inherently NP-hard and involves complex energy-related operational constraints. Existing approaches often rely either on exact methods, which scale poorly for industrial-sized instances, or on heuristic methods that can rapidly generate feasible schedules but often with high energy consumption. To address these limitations, we develop a hybrid energy-efficient scheduling approach that integrates gene expression programming (GEP), local search, and mathematical programming. Within the proposed framework, GEP is employed to generate machine allocation and operation sequencing decisions, the local search algorithm further improves the generated schedules, and mathematical programming subsequently refines the solutions to enhance optimality. Benchmark evaluations demonstrate that the proposed hybrid approach consistently yields lower energy consumption than the existing GEP approach, the mathematical programming model, and the decomposition-based approach in most instances, with energy consumption reductions of up to 16.1%, 44.9% and 19.0%, respectively.

Predictive fluid–property modeling of supercritical power cycle performance using the Extended Corresponding States framework
abstract: This paper presents a predictive framework for evaluating how thermophysical fluid properties influence the performance of supercritical Brayton and recuperated power cycles. Understanding these relationships is essential for developing high-efficiency energy systems and extending cycle design beyond well-characterized CO 2 and CO 2 -based mixtures. Leveraging Extended Corresponding States (ECS) theory, the study establishes a physically interpretable, data-driven model that links fluid properties to thermodynamic cycle efficiency across a broad range of synthetic and real working fluids. A large dataset of ECS-generated fluids is created by varying nine independent thermophysical parameters within physically meaningful bounds and coupling them with a systematic sweep of operating conditions, including pressure ratio, turbine inlet temperature, and component isentropic efficiencies. Cycle simulations are performed for both Brayton and recuperated configurations, and the resulting data are analyzed using statistically validated regression models to quantify the influence of fluid and operating parameters on thermal efficiency. The results show that operating parameters dominate overall performance, with pressure ratio and isentropic efficiencies being most influential in Brayton cycles, while pressure ratio, isentropic efficiency, and turbine inlet temperature dominate in recuperated cycles. Fluid–property effects govern efficiency trends primarily through the ideal-gas specific heat capacity, its temperature dependence, and the critical temperature (for recuperated cycles). The model accurately predicts performance trends across real fluids within the validated ECS evaluation domain and captures the key thermophysical dependencies governing both cycle configurations. The resulting generalized fluid–property–performance relationships provide a physically interpretable framework for working-fluid pre-selection and cycle optimization of supercritical power systems.

An effective bi-level optimization approach for the management of energy communities
abstract: Energy communities are expected to play a key role in the energy transition by supporting the deployment of renewable energy technologies. Their full potential can be unlocked through coordinated operation, typically managed by an aggregator. However, centralized approaches raise concerns regarding privacy, computational scalability, and the conflicting objectives of the community participants. To address these challenges, this work proposes a bi-level optimization framework for the operational management of energy communities. The formulation is based on a single-leader, multiple-followers Stackelberg game, in which the aggregator determines the internal electricity purchase and selling prices, while the community members independently optimize the operation of their local energy systems, including photovoltaic generation, battery energy storage, and flexible demand. The upper-level problem is solved using an evolutionary algorithm tailored for non-smooth problems, while the lower-level problems are solved to optimality using linear or mixed-integer linear programming. The framework supports both centralized and distributed implementations, preserving prosumer privacy by exchanging only price signals and electricity import/export schedules. The proposed approach is evaluated on several homogeneous and heterogeneous energy community configurations with realistic load profiles. The results show that the proposed framework achieves economic performance close to that of a centralized benchmark while significantly reducing the total operating cost compared with uncoordinated operation. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the upper-level objective function can be adapted to improve the distribution of economic benefits among community members, highlighting the flexibility of the proposed optimization framework.

Integrating electricity demand, hydrogen production, and renewable energy sources: Techno-economic assessment at Milan Malpensa International Airport
abstract: Aviation is considered one of the key hard-to-abate sectors. Hydrogen produced from renewable energy can play a central role in enabling low-carbon airport operations in the present and for hydrogen-powered aircraft in the future. This study presents a comprehensive techno-economic assessment of on-site renewable hydrogen production for Milan Malpensa International Airport, analyzing the optimal sizing of a hybrid photovoltaic (PV) and wind Renewable Energy Source (RES) plant and alkaline electrolyzer systems. Grounded on one year of high-resolution measured airport electricity demand (12.0 MW average load; 105.4 GWh annual consumption) and synthetic renewable generation profiles, a rule-based energy dispatch algorithm evaluates key performance indicators across four plant configurations. Benchmark dedicated hydrogen production yields a minimum levelized cost of hydrogen of 5.16 €/kg at optimal PV-to-electrolyzer ( P / E = 2.26 ) and wind-to-electrolyzer ( W / E = 1.58 ) ratios. In a shared RES framework supplying both airport baseload and the electrolyzer, optimal renewable energy sources power-to-load ( R / L ) and electrolyzer-to-load ( E / L ) ratios follow linear correlation trends dependent on renewable share. Minimum levelized cost of hydrogen ranges from 5.10 €/kg for 100% PV ( E / L = 13.7 , R / L = 36.0 ) to 6.10 €/kg for 100% wind ( E / L = 11.7 , R / L = 39.4 ), while a balanced 50% PV/50% wind configuration achieves 5.30 €/kg ( E / L = 7.37 , R / L = 28.7 ). At production scales reaching up to 10.5 kton/year of H 2 , the dual-purpose shared system reduces total annual energy expenses by up to 2.9 M€ when comparing with a scenario where renewable energy and renewable hydrogen are produced with two dedicated plants, and up to 7.8 M€ when comparing to a more traditional scenario relying on grid electricity together with a dedicated renewable hydrogen plant. This work also lays the foundation for a replicable assessment of the proposed shared renewable plant for clean hydrogen and energy production. In fact, the presented framework is based on generalized dimensionless parameters that could be used to characterize other airports of different sizes and locations as well as other hard-to-abate industrial sectors, finally enabling scalable assessment of renewable-hydrogen integration strategies.
