abstract: Wind energy has been recognized as a promising energy source for broadly distributed electronics, due to its widespread availability and sustainability. Vertical axis wind turbines (VAWTs) are more suitable for harvesting wind energy in urban environments compared to horizontal axis wind turbines (HAWTs), owing to their omni-directional, low noise emission and lightweight characteristics. In our previous study, a novel VAWT with adaptive blades (consisting of flaps that open and close in response to the flow conditions) has been designed and constructed. The current study extends our previous study by further improving the rotor performance and by investigating the operating mechanism of the adaptive rotor. Wind tunnel experiments were conducted to compare the conventional rotor and the adaptive rotor under different wind speeds. The effects of inclination and pitch angle on the aerodynamic performance were investigated, and a favourable pitch angle of −8° was identified under the adjustable-beam configuration at 6 m/s. Based on this selected angle configuration, the improved rotor increased the maximum power coefficient from below 5% in the previous prototype to approximately 11% at 6 m/s, and reduced the self-starting wind speed from 8 m/s to 4 m/s. With this configuration, the adaptive blades further improved the low-speed torque performance compared with the conventional blades, increasing the minimum torque coefficient by 23% at 6 m/s, and thereby accelerating the self-starting process, while maintaining a comparable maximum power coefficient at high rotation speeds. However, the adaptive blades did not further reduce the self-starting wind speed. The analysis indicates that the transition rotation speed (representing the transition from drag-based to lift-based operation) of the adaptive blade is a key factor for further improvement.

Energy crisis and the renewable-to-fossil energy balance in the European Union: Linear and nonlinear evidence, 2009–2024
abstract: Energy crises may either delay or accelerate the transition from fossil fuels to renewable energy, but the direction of the relationship remains unsettled. This study examines the association between energy-crisis intensity and the renewable-to-fossil energy ratio in 21 European Union countries during 2009–2024. A composite crisis index combines fossil-fuel consumption growth, electricity-price growth, fossil-fuel import dependence, realized declines in physical fossil-fuel imports, and energy inflation. Panel ARDL estimators, common correlated effects mean group (CCEMG), DOLS, FMOLS, a fixed-effects threshold model, and the Juodis–Karavias–Sarafidis predictive test are used. The preferred PMG estimate is negative, and DFE, CCEMG, DOLS, and FMOLS have the same direction; however, the MG estimate is statistically insignificant, and the CCEMG coefficient becomes insignificant when 2021–2022 are excluded. The linear result is therefore neither estimator- nor episode-invariant. The threshold model identifies a tentative, sample-specific regime boundary: the association is negative below it and positive above it. Because the dependent variable is a ratio, a higher value may reflect renewable expansion, fossil-fuel contraction, or both. The one-lag predictive test indicates feedback in both directions, whereas at two lags only crisis-to-ratio predictability remains; neither result establishes structural causality. The results reconcile the barrier and catalyst interpretations of energy crises while showing that policy recommendations concerning grids, storage, and permitting are interpretive implications rather than directly estimated infrastructure effects.

abstract: Systems proposed in this paper fully integrate the needs and trends of the present energy system development by combining the use of renewable energy sources, the utilization of carbon dioxide, and energy storage using liquid and gaseous fuels. The paper introduces two main systems for synthetic fuel production, both based on the processes of biomass gasification and electrolysis. The first case assumes synthetic natural gas (SNG) production by syngas hydrogenation via methanation process. The second case assumes liquid synthetic fuel (syncrude) production by syngas hydrogenation via Fischer-Tropsch (FT) synthesis. Both systems were analyzed for two types of electrolysis process – Anion Exchange Membrane Electrolyzer (AEMEL), and Solid Oxide Electrolyzer (SOEL). The system efficiency and economic potential of SNG and FT fuels production systems is presented in this work. The systems were analyzed for various design conditions such as temperature and pressure, and different H2:CO, and H2:CO2 ratios. The calculated system performance of proposed synfuel production systems is 55.66% for SNG production and 42.07% for syncrude production and improves up to 66.72% and 53.56%, respectively, with efficient heat integration and the use of high-temperature electrolysis. A sensitivity analysis was conducted to determine the break-even price of SNG and FT products, considering different scenarios for the costs of feedstock. The analysis shows that fuel production costs are highly sensitive to the price of renewable electricity, with the calculated break-even price for SNG ranging from 28.7 – 149.0 €/MWh and 77.3 – 280.3 €/MWh (0.49 – 1.77 €/l) for syncrude.

District heating decarbonization pathways for cold-climate urban energy Systems: The case of Helsinki
abstract: Decarbonising district heating in cold-climate cities requires long-term emissions reduction without compromising heat supply during prolonged winter peaks. This study develops a discrete planning envelope for the Helsinki metropolitan district-heating system using hourly EnergyPLAN simulations of 45 unique configurations for 2019–2040. The analysis combines policy-linked milestones with technology scans covering heat pumps, electric boilers, thermal energy storage (TES), waste heat, offshore wind, and electricity storage. Across the main pathway, fossil-fuel use falls from 6.59 TWh a -1 to zero and gross model-accounted CO 2 emissions from 1.521 Mt a -1 to zero. However, the 2040 core configuration still records 269.833 GWh of energy not supplied over 465 h, with a peak deficit of 2155 MW, showing that annual decarbonisation does not ensure winter adequacy. The heat-pump–TES scan reveals nonlinear cost and adequacy responses: heat pumps provide the main electricity-to-heat conversion flexibility, whereas larger TES improves peak-period security but raises annualised cost. Increasing offshore wind lowers export-corrected emissions but increases exports and critical excess electricity production, while expanding electricity storage from 0.1 to 1 GWh reduces CEEP by only 3.1 percentage points and does not improve heat adequacy. Meeting a strict zero-ENS criterion for the 2040 pathway requires approximately 2.2 GW th of low-utilisation firm heat capacity, increasing the annualised system cost by about 16% relative to the unscreened 2040 configuration. The results show that cold-climate district-heating planning should coordinate electrified heat production, storage, recovered heat, and firm winter capacity, and evaluate candidate pathways using hourly adequacy alongside cost and emissions.

abstract: Integrating renewable energy into residential buildings is challenging in cold regions, where solar resources are limited and growing electric vehicle (EV) adoption increases grid load. This study aims to promote circularity in the building energy system by using locally generated renewable energy to supply both residential electricity demand and EV charging demand, thereby reducing dependence on the grid. The optimal sizing of a grid-connected hybrid system combining photovoltaic (PV) panels, wind turbines (WT), and battery storage is addressed for an EV-integrated residential building in two contrasting Finnish climates: humid continental Helsinki and subarctic Oulu. Since the sizing problem is nonlinear and multidimensional, five metaheuristic algorithms from evolutionary, swarm intelligence, and bio-inspired families, namely Genetic Algorithm, Whale Optimization Algorithm, Ant Lion Optimizer, Dragonfly Algorithm, and Grey Wolf Optimizer, are benchmarked to identify the best-performing algorithm. The Whale Optimization Algorithm achieves the lowest cost together with one of the fastest convergence behaviors among the tested algorithms, whereas the Dragonfly Algorithm yields the highest cost. In Helsinki, the optimal hybrid PV and WT configuration reaches an energy cost of 0.10 USD/kWh, about 52% renewable penetration, and over 48% CO 2 reduction, while the PV-only system in Oulu reaches 0.13 USD/kWh, about 19% renewable penetration, and about 18% CO 2 reduction. Sensitivity analysis shows that EV charging from 00:00 to 08:00 minimizes total system cost in both cities, while shifting EV demand to midday in Helsinki, when combined PV and wind output exceeds local demand, reduces curtailed excess electricity by about 16%.

title: Toward green and intelligent marine power systems: A systematic review of modeling and simulation technologies
Benchmarking Solar-Optimized Electric Vehicle Charging Systems: An Open and Reproducible Evaluation Method
abstract: This work presents an open and reproducible evaluation method for benchmarking solar-optimized electric vehicle (EV) charging systems in residential applications. While solar charging is increasingly adopted, there is currently no transparent and technology-independent approach for objectively comparing the performance of different charging systems. This work addresses this gap by combining a unified performance indicator (PI) with a validated simulation model, enabling reproducible benchmarking under identical boundary conditions.,Five commercially available EV charging systems were characterized through laboratory measurements following established testing procedures and subsequently represented by a parameterized simulation model. The model is released together with example datasets to enable reproducible benchmarking under identical boundary conditions.,The proposed PI quantifies both additional grid consumption and excess feed-in relative to an idealized control behavior, enabling a holistic assessment of system performance. Results show that the simulation reproduces the main control characteristics of the investigated systems with sufficient accuracy. The comparative analysis reveals PI values ranging from approximately 83% to over 95%, corresponding to notable economic differences. The decomposition of the PI identifies the dominant loss mechanisms, including control delays, transient behavior, phase-switching constraints, and standby consumption, thereby enabling targeted optimization of charger control strategies. The proposed methodology further proves sufficiently sensitive to quantify performance improvements resulting from charger redesigns. However, the proposed method provides a transferable and reproducible basis for benchmarking solar-optimized EV charging systems, supporting transparent comparison, future controller development, and independent performance assessment.

abstract: This study proposes an innovative geothermal exploration system that combines an enhanced geothermal system (EGS) and a closed coaxial heat exchanger geothermal system (CCGS) for heat extraction in discrete fracture networks and coaxial wells. Firstly, a mathematical model was established, considering the fluid flow and heat transfer processes in fractures, reservoir matrix, and wellbores. Subsequently, an analysis was conducted to examine the temperature and velocity contours in discrete fracture networks and coaxial wells. Moreover, the heat extraction performance of the proposed EGS-CCGS was compared with that of a traditional EGS. Finally, the key factors affecting heat production were discussed and analyzed. The results showed that the CCGS can significantly enhance the heat extraction efficiency of fractured geothermal systems. When fracture connectivity is suboptimal, the heat extraction efficiency for the system can be improved by up to 150%. The optimal injection rates for the combined EGS-CCGS system are 120 kg/s for the EGS and 25 kg/s for the CCGS. When the fracture connectivity is low, the rock matrix thermal conductivity has a significant impact on heat extraction efficiency, while the fracture permeability has a relatively minor effect. Conversely, the opposite effects are reported when the fracture connectivity is high.

abstract: Concentrating solar technologies (CST) have shown a wide potential for power generation at highly-irradiated locations and for thermochemical processes and industrial heat production. In particular, solar power tower (SPT) systems are especially effective for high temperature applications. However, a techno-economical gap in terms of operation and maintenance, flux and meteorological conditions’ monitoring, and plant control still hinders the serial industrial adoption of this energy source. In order to tailor an embedded solution for flux prediction and control, this work presents the simulation-to-reality learning step of an Attention-Gated U-Net (AttU-Net) model especially tailored for flux density prediction. This neural network, previously trained with a purely synthetic dataset, has been re-trained with an experimental dataset composed of 562 samples, which was obtained between May 2025, and July 2025. The training results show solid accuracies above 95%, structural similarity indexes (SSIM) up to 97% and peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) metrics over 30 dB, which is consistent with model robustness and accuracy. Inference ability and times were tested with 10 held-out samples, reaching accuracies above 96%, SSIMs above 92%, as well as PSNRs above 30 dB. These results suggest the algorithm’s suitability for future integration within flux density control loops to improve plant operability and safety.

abstract: Ammonia–hydrogen blends are promising carbon-free fuels for net-zero energy systems, yet their equilibrium thermochemical behavior across wide operating conditions remains insufficiently mapped. This study establishes a parameter-resolved ideal-gas equilibrium map for NH 3 –H 2 –air mixtures over 0–100 mol% H 2 on a molar fuel basis, equivalence ratios of 0.3–2.0, pressures of 1–60 atm, and unburned-mixture temperatures of 300–800 K. The study provides a system-specific and reproducible thermodynamic dataset that: (i) quantifies the coupled adiabatic flame temperature (AFT)– c p –composition response; (ii) identifies lean, near-stoichiometric, and rich equilibrium regimes; (iii) relates blend composition to lower heating value (LHV)-based fuel-flow requirements; and (iv) benchmarks the retained 11-species formulation against NASA Chemical Equilibrium with Applications (CEA) calculations. Over 225 benchmark cases, the mean absolute error (MAE) and root-mean-square error (RMSE) in AFT were 1.61 and 2.07 K, respectively, with a maximum absolute error of 5.85 K; the corresponding MAE for equilibrium c p was 0.00511 kJ kg -1 K -1 . An unrestricted CEA assessment over the same grid was additionally used to quantify the adequacy of the retained species set. Hydrogen enrichment raised both flame temperature and equilibrium heat-capacity demand; at 600 K and 60 atm, increasing H 2 from 0 to 100 mol% increased AFT by 379 K. Pressure moderated dissociation: for pure H 2 at 300 K, increasing pressure from 1 to 60 atm reduced equilibrium c p by 24.8% while increasing AFT by 3.9%. Equivalence ratio organized the map into lean oxidation-controlled, near-stoichiometric pressure-sensitive, and rich oxygen-limited regimes. Rich operation reduced the equilibrium NO marker but lowered AFT and increased residual-H 2 retention. The map provides thermodynamic screening boundaries for subsequent gas-turbine, engine-cycle, finite-rate kinetic, computational fluid dynamics (CFD), and experimental studies, rather than direct combustor-design or emissions predictions.

abstract: Solar-driven solid desiccant dehumidification systems have attracted considerable attention as an energy-efficient and environmentally friendly alternative to conventional vapor-compression dehumidification, owing to their ability to utilize low-grade solar thermal energy and reduce electricity consumption. However, their widespread application remains constrained by the complexity and cost associated with integrating solar collectors. This paper presents the design and optimization of a novel, multi-blade-damper-shaped solar dehumidification module (MBD-SDM) that directly absorbs solar radiation inside the module and eliminates the need for external collectors. The transient performance is investigated through multiphysics simulations. The desiccant configurations, specifically desiccant thickness and gap width, along with operational air flow rates, are systematically evaluated. Results indicate that the D3/G3 configuration (3 mm desiccant thickness with a 1:1 thickness-to-gap ratio) balances dehumidification and regeneration performance enhancement against pressure drop, requiring negligible fan power. Furthermore, a dehumidification air flow rate of 50–100 m 3 /h is recommended to optimize moisture removal performance, yielding peak M R R values of 0.0516–0.0894 g/s. Meanwhile, an optimal regeneration air flow rate of 5 m 3 /h achieves a cumulative average solar regeneration efficiency of 34.9% over a 60-min cycle under a solar irradiance of 1000 W/m 2 . The results highlight the system's ability to provide compact, efficient, and continuous dehumidification.

abstract: This study presents a comparative techno-economic and environmental assessment of four solid oxide fuel cell (SOFC)-based marine power systems fuelled by methanol, ammonia and hydrogen. The systems are sized to meet the 34.30 MW power demand of a reference container ship and comprise a methanol-fuelled SOFC (System A); a methanol-fuelled SOFC coupled to a molten carbonate fuel cell (MCFC) and organic Rankine cycle (ORC) with onboard CO 2 capture and liquefaction (System B); an ammonia-fuelled SOFC–ORC (System C); and a hydrogen-fuelled SOFC–ORC (System D). In System B, the MCFC uses the SOFC exhaust as its cathode feed and concentrates CO 2 in the anode exhaust while also generating additional power; the concentrated CO 2 stream is then conditioned and liquefied. System D achieved the highest energy and exergy efficiencies (73.29% and 75.11%), while System A yielded the lowest levelised cost of electricity (0.0969 £/kWh). System B reduced the specific CO 2 emission factor from 511.7 to 23.88 gCO 2 /kWh, corresponding to a 95.3% reduction relative to reference engine system, and achieved the lowest cost of CO 2 avoided (93.6 £/tCO 2 ), with a cargo-space penalty of 0.92–4.60% for 7–35-day offloading intervals. Fuel cost accounts for 62–85% of total annual expenditure, making delivered fuel price the main determinant of economic competitiveness. Methanol-fuelled SOFCs are the most cost-effective near-term option, hydrogen gives the highest thermodynamic performance, and the SOFC–MCFC–ORC configuration provides the deepest onboard CO 2 reduction where the cargo-space penalty is within operational limits.

An integrated framework for evaluating tidal stream generation potential and its power system benefits: evidence from Great Britain
abstract: This paper presents an integrated framework that combines geospatial analysis with power system modelling to evaluate the optimal deployment and system-level value of tidal stream generation in Great Britain (GB). High-resolution geospatial screening – based on tidal maximum current velocity (≥ 2.5 m/s), mean tidal speeds (≥ 1.5 m/s) water depth (35–45 m and 30–50 m), and distance to shore (≤ 50 km) – is coupled with a multi-objective NSGA-II optimisation to identify Pareto-optimal sites for tidal stream development. The results indicate that promising locations are concentrated in a limited number of high-resource coastal regions, notably around the Orkney Islands and Pentland Firth, the Anglesey and North Wales coastline, and the Bristol Channel. These sites are subsequently incorporated into a 17-zone representation of the 2030 GB electricity system using the PyPSA model. Simulation results show that deploying 1.5 GW of tidal stream capacity – on an energy-equivalent basis in place of wind and solar PV – reduces variable renewable curtailment by 0.6 TWh, displaces a comparable volume of gas-fired generation, and lowers total system operating costs by £65 million per year. Furthermore, analysis of electricity market impacts indicates reductions in average generation costs of up to £1.0/MWh in high-cost zones, alongside relatively stable technology-specific market capture prices for tidal stream generation compared to wind and solar. The proposed framework is modular and scalable, making it applicable to other coastal regions and power systems using location-specific datasets and scenarios.

title: Academic landscape on sharing renewable and waste heat in active district heating: A systematic literature review
abstract: The heating and cooling sector accounts for a significant share of energy consumption and greenhouse gas emissions, and district heating and cooling (DHC) systems are seen as promising decarbonisation solutions, requiring their renovation and evolution toward more flexible and integrated configurations. Decarbonising DHC requires integrating renewable energy and waste heat, reducing fossil fuel dependence and increasing community engagement. Bidirectional flows and prosumers should be further explored to enhance system flexibility, as these concepts are well established in electricity but still underexplored in thermal systems. This work focuses on the emerging set of approaches aimed at decarbonising District Heating systems, collectively referred to as Active District Heating (ADH), through a systematic review of 171 scientific articles. The study provides a clear conceptual framework to analyse how the research community approaches ADH models, structuring the literature across methodological approaches, technologies, digitalisation tools, and regulatory aspects. The results indicate that ADH is emerging as a flexible, digitalised, and potentially bidirectional network paradigm, largely established at the theoretical level, with 76% of studies based on modelling and simulation, while practical applications in real systems or pilot-scale demonstrations remain limited (11%). The literature is strongly concentrated in Europe (85%), with key enabling solutions including waste heat recovery (48%), heat pumps (39%), and solar thermal collectors (33%), while around 20% of studies analyse the end-user–network interface for thermal prosumers. Finally, regulatory uncertainty and the lack of clear third-party access mechanisms, together with geographical and policy disparities, are identified as the main barriers affecting ADH development.

What is a “Thermonet”? Positioning ground-coupled cold networks among low-temperature district heating configurations and business models
abstract: Thermonet is a Danish term for shared networks near ground temperature linking buildings to the ground and other low-grade sources. Its relation to district energy is unclear. Using 24 operating cases in Denmark and Sweden, this paper establishes what the thermonet denotes in practice and how its meaning has been formed. Cases were classified by network configuration and business model, and the term's emergence was traced over time. All cases are cold networks with heat pumps at or close to the buildings; most Danish cases are heating-led near ground temperature, and most Swedish cases recover heat or supply cooling. The cases depart from the business model expected for low-temperature district heating mainly in customers and customer relationships, since users often own the system. Social value lay mainly in sharing local heat and energy, while carefree supply depended on who managed the heat pumps. The meaning of the term has shifted, with consequences for how thermonets are regulated and financed. Early uses placed heat pumps in each building, and by 2024 practitioners also admitted central heat pumps and sought recognition as district heating. The Danish state instead classified the thermonet with individual heating and from 2025 excluded building heat pump installations from collective heat supply and municipal loan guarantees, fixing the earlier meaning in law. Practitioners now define the thermonet without reference to heat pumps. In practice, the thermonet is organisationally new, combining a known cold network type with a distinctive allocation of ownership and responsibility, while its definition remains contested.

title: Structural optimization and variable operating condition simulation of concentrated solar-driven atmospheric water harvester
Stochastic model predictive control for PV–BESS microgrid energy management under demand charge
abstract: Behind-the-meter microgrid energy management faces a fundamental temporal discrepancy: real-time control decisions at 15-minute resolution must account for financial penalties consolidated over 30-day billing cycles. Under hybrid tariff structures combining time-of-use charges with monthly peak demand penalties, costs are assessed against the highest 15-minute average power within the billing month, rendering standard short-horizon controllers prone to sub-optimality. This paper proposes a Stochastic Model Predictive Control (SMPC) architecture that resolves this conflict by integrating a discrete historical peak state variable into a receding-horizon Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulation, coupling each dispatch decision to the accumulated demand exposure of the active billing cycle. Control actions are restricted to Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) dispatch, excluding load shedding and solar curtailment. Forecast uncertainty for load and photovoltaic generation is quantified via a hybrid probabilistic framework: a conformal-prediction-calibrated XGBoost model produces 90% confidence intervals for load demand, while a four-model numerical weather prediction ensemble bounds solar generation uncertainty. Real-time forecast mismatches are mitigated through asymmetric bias correction and adaptive scenario reweighting. Validated on empirical data from a medium-voltage university campus microgrid as a case study, the proposed SMPC achieves a 12.57% cost reduction relative to the unmanaged baseline. A Perfect Foresight MPC sensitivity analysis isolates the cost of load forecasting uncertainty to 1.21%, confirming that residual sub-optimality is driven primarily by the finite prediction horizon and solar stochasticity rather than load forecast inaccuracy.

An innovative high-temperature subcritical pumped thermal energy storage system using biphenyl-diphenyl oxide mixture
abstract: Recently, high-temperature pumped thermal energy storage (PTES) operating at 400-600 °C has garnered widespread attention, with several projects successfully launched due to its high energy storage density and ability to provide electricity or high-quality steam. Nevertheless, a range of limitations exists, including substantial work input for gas compression, high capital expenditure and operational pressures, huge equipment and irreversible losses. To alleviate these challenges, this study introduces a novel high-temperature subcritical PTES system based on a biphenyl-diphenyl oxide (BDO) mixture. The dual-tank configuration utilizing BDO enables an extreme heat-storage temperature of 395 °C, while the maximum system operating pressure is only approximately 1 MPa. The BDO also serves as the working fluid for both the heat-pump charging cycle and the power-generation discharging cycle of the PTES. This unified-working-fluid design greatly reduces heat transfer losses. The results reveal that a higher inlet temperature of waste heat flue gas improves the system performance. Conversely, an increase in flue gas mass flow rate reduces both the coefficient of performance (COP) and round-trip efficiency ( ). The maximum reaches 641.62%, with a corresponding COP of 22.71. For a 6-hour heat discharge duration, the levelized cost of storage is 0.369 $/kWh and energy storage density is 27.735 kWh/m 3 .

Provincial pathways for decarbonizing China's steel sector through electricity and hydrogen substitution
abstract: ABSTRACT The deep decarbonization of China’s steel sector is critical for achieving national carbon neutrality and global climate goals. Existing studies on China’s steel transition often lack detailed representations of provincial heterogeneity, cross-sectoral interactions, and breakthrough technologies. This study develops an improved steel module within the Global Change Analysis Model-China (GCAM-China) to explore provincial low-carbon transition pathways for China’s steel sector. The model incorporates calibrated steel demand, multiple breakthrough technologies, and province-specific resource endowments and technology costs, enabling a more realistic representation of provincial transition dynamics and explicit interactions among the steel, power, and hydrogen systems. The results show that China’s steel sector is projected to undergo a structural transition toward electric arc furnace (EAF)-based and hydrogen-based steelmaking pathways. Electricity and hydrogen play critical roles in enabling deep decarbonization through the transformation of upstream energy systems. The combined share of EAF-based and hydrogen-based steelmaking exceeds 80% by 2060, replacing coal-intensive routes and reducing CO 2 emissions by more than 90% relative to 2020 levels, with residual emissions of 60–126 MtCO 2 under carbon neutrality scenarios. Provincial transitions show significant heterogeneity, with southern provinces favoring Scrap-EAF deployment, northern provinces favoring natural gas-based direct reduced iron-EAF (NG-DRI-EAF) deployment, southwestern provinces benefiting from electricity–hydrogen synergies, and eastern, southern, and southwestern provinces showing higher potential for molten oxide electrolysis (MOE) deployment. By integrating national transition dynamics with provincial characteristics, this study provides insights for differentiated policy design and supports more targeted deployment of technologies and infrastructure across regions.

Resilient renewable-integrated hydrogen refueling for urban bus fleets: Wasserstein-regularized multi-horizon control
abstract: Renewable-integrated hydrogen refueling stations (HRSs) must coordinate intermittent generation, clustered bus demand, variable prices, and delayed procurement while maintaining dispenser-side service. This paper develops a Wasserstein-regularized multi-horizon model predictive control framework (WDR–MHMPC) for supervisory operation of a single HRS serving urban and regional fuel-cell bus fleets. The application-specific framework integrates topology-consistent routing, class-specific main tanks, a market-interface backup tank, a fuel-cell buffer tank, and a finite delivery pipeline with ambiguity-aware reserve shaping and multi-horizon blocking; unarrived hydrogen is excluded from on-site inventory. The type-1 Wasserstein term regularizes the affine uncertainty sensitivity of the nonanticipative loss, while physical constraints remain trajectory-wise. Validation uses source-calibrated synthetic renewable, demand, price, and logistics profiles in a seven-day calibration and controller comparison, a 30-day stress case, and a 100-week seeded ensemble. In the primary week, WDR–MHMPC supplies the complete 14.37 t demand with zero reserve-target-exposure hours, matching WDR–SHMPC in service reliability. Relative to WDR–SHMPC, it reduces the priced operating-value ledger from 90.144 to 73.608 kUSD/week and the service-adjusted evaluation cost from 94.791 to 80.224 kUSD/week, reductions of 18.3% and 15.4%, respectively. Across the 100 supplied weeks, WDR–MHMPC records zero unserved hydrogen, with mean and maximum reserve-target exposures of 1.66 and 9 h/week. Multi-horizon blocking reduces the slow-decision parameterization from H p n s to ( H r + N b ) n s . These simulations support reliable supervisory service and lower evaluation cost for the tested configuration, but do not establish field performance, recursive feasibility, closed-loop stability, or authenticated real-time solver performance.

Temporally-Conditioned Diffusion Transformer for appliance-level load synthesis in Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring
abstract: Non-Intrusive Load Monitoring (NILM) provides appliance-level energy visibility for intelligent building energy management, but deep NILM models remain constrained by limited appliance-level training data and severe class imbalance from sparse appliance activations. Generative data augmentation can alleviate this bottleneck; however, existing NILM generators mainly reproduce appliance waveform morphology or isolated active-event segments, while often neglecting the temporal usage context needed for realistic continuous appliance sequences. To address this gap, this paper formulates NILM data augmentation as a temporally conditioned continuous load synthesis problem and proposes the Temporally-Conditioned Diffusion Transformer (TC-DiT). TC-DiT integrates a DiT-based diffusion-transformer architecture with decoupled multivariate diffusion, AdaLN-Zero temporal conditioning, and active-event continuity enhancement to generate continuous appliance power trajectories that preserve stochastic power dynamics while aligning activations with calendar-derived temporal context. Evaluations on the UK-DALE dataset show that TC-DiT improves waveform fidelity, temporal alignment, and joint power-temporal consistency compared with Generative Adversarial Network (GAN), Time-series Generative Adversarial Network (TimeGAN), and Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM)-Decoupled. Under a Train-on-Real-plus-Synthetic, Test-on-Real (TRSTR) protocol, selecting the best-performing synthetic injection ratio for each appliance-window setting reduces average Mean Absolute Error (MAE) by 18.8% and increases Matching Rate (MR) by 10.9 percentage points over three independent runs; under a fixed global 100% synthetic injection ratio, TC-DiT still achieves a 15.8% MAE reduction and a 9.2 percentage-point MR gain. These results indicate that time-context-aware synthetic load profiles improve downstream NILM performance in the evaluated UK-DALE cross-house setting under data-scarce and class-imbalanced conditions.

Thermal energy storage and district heating as flexibility enablers for industrial heat decarbonization
abstract: Electrifying industrial process heat production links industrial decarbonization to power-system constraints, increasing the need for flexibility. We apply an integrated energy system model, coupling industrial heat demands with district heating systems, to quantify how thermal energy storage (TES) and heat exchange with district heating affect cost-optimal decarbonization pathways for a region in Germany. We investigate the investments required in the transition towards a fully decarbonized energy system, including energy storage, heat pumps and renewable electricity generation, from today to 2050 with tightening emission restrictions. Results show that TES lowers total system costs by 6%–12% and reduces wind and solar curtailment, thereby substituting up to 36% of the cost-optimal battery capacity. In industry, low-temperature TES is deployed in early investment periods to even out heat pump operation and reduce the required heat pump capacity. On the other hand, high-temperature TES becomes relevant in later, highly electrified periods to time-shift power-intensive heat production under grid constraints. Coupling industry and district heating reduces the need for low-temperature storage by sharing heat across sectors, and unlocks more efficient process electrification by providing a heat source for high-temperature heat pumps. This leads to heat exchange between industry and district heating shifting from net export from industry in early periods to net import under tight emission constraints.

A Nonlinear Model Predictive Control framework for TEC-based BTMS in Light Electric Vehicles
abstract: This paper presents a Nonlinear Model Predictive Control (NLMPC) strategy for the energy-efficient thermal management of Light Electric Vehicle (LEV) batteries using Thermoelectric Coolers (TECs). While LEVs feature compact battery packs with small thermal masses, TECs provide a solid-state, space-efficient cooling solution ideal for this platform. However, TECs act as a parasitic load, drawing energy from the battery and increasing internal heat generation. While linear Model Predictive Control (MPC) strategies have been considered, their reliance on a model linearized around a specific operating point renders them inadequate for the strong, non-linear dynamics of a TEC-BTMS. A full NLMPC strategy, despite its theoretical superiority, has not yet been applied to this problem. Furthermore, existing controllers ignore the parasitic load of TECs, which draws energy from the battery, thereby increasing the heat generation. To address this, the NLMPC’s internal model is developed to explicitly couple the TEC’s parasitic load with the battery’s heat generation. Simulations show that the NLMPC controller provides a 47.3% to 74.2% reduction in energy usage compared to a relay controller across all tested conditions. Compared to the Proportional-Integral-Derivative (PID) controller tuned at an ambient temperature of 25 °C, the NLMPC provides similar energy consumption while at higher ambient temperatures it saves up to 51.8% energy. The novel parasitic load coupling of TECs within the NLMPC accounts for up to 25% energy saving from baseline NLMPC. The results demonstrate that NLMPC significantly enhances both thermal management and energy efficiency, addressing key challenges in LEV battery systems and extending vehicle range.

title: Spatio-temporal characterisation of diurnal renewable generation patterns using functional principal component analysis
abstract: In power systems with high renewable penetration, the spatial allocation of weather-dependent resources directly affects system reliability and operational costs. Since electricity demand follows a diurnal pattern, the daily shape of renewable generation determines its contribution to the residual demand profile. However, existing resource characterisation metrics, based on annual potential and variability, carry no information about the daily generation profile shape. This study presents a statistical methodology for the spatio-temporal characterisation of diurnal renewable generation patterns and the clustering of regions with similar patterns. Functional Principal Component Analysis is applied to daily generation profiles to extract the dominant diurnal modes shared across a region, with scores quantifying the expression of each mode per location and day. Feature-based K-means clustering of the mean scores at each location then delineates regions of similar diurnal behaviour. Results are presented for an hourly wind power dataset comprising 10 850 locations in the Western Cape supply region of South Africa over five years. Four components account for 86.2% of the variation about the mean daily profile. The dominant diurnal modes reveal pronounced differences, not captured by annual resource metrics, in the diurnal generation of locations with comparable energy yield, most notably during the evening peak-demand period. The clustering delineates spatially coherent regions of similar diurnal generation behaviour. The proposed approach enables energy planners to characterise diurnal generation patterns across a region in an interpretable, compact form and to identify regions that serve as inputs to long-term planning models.

Integration of third-generation concentrated solar power and solid oxide electrolysis for dispatchable solar hydrogen production: Multi-variable optimization and techno-economic assessment
abstract: This study presents a third-generation (Gen3) concentrated solar power (CSP) system integrated with solid oxide electrolysis cells (SOECs) for dispatchable hydrogen production. The configuration combines a liquid sodium central receiver, ternary chloride molten salt (MgCl 2 -KCl-NaCl) thermal energy storage, a recompression supercritical CO 2 Brayton cycle operating at 700°C, and an SOEC at 800°C. System performance is evaluated using an integrated thermodynamic, exergy, exergoeconomic, and techno-economic framework under Almería, Spain conditions (direct normal irradiance, DNI, 2240 kWh/m 2 /yr). The baseline system achieves a 69.5% capacity factor, substantially exceeding typical second-generation CSP plants, with overall energy and exergy efficiencies of 24.2% and 25.7%, respectively. Component-level exergoeconomic analysis identifies the SOEC stack and receiver assembly as dominant cost drivers, confirming that capital cost reduction is the primary improvement pathway. Multi-variable genetic algorithm optimization identifies a global optimum achieving a levelized cost of hydrogen (LCOH 2 ) of 3.84 $/kg at a 70.9% capacity factor. Techno-economic assessment shows that electricity cost is the dominant economic driver: reducing it from 55.66 to 20 $/MWh lowers LCOH 2 by approximately 1.19 $/kg, more than three times the benefit achievable through complete SOEC maturation by 2050. Net present value (NPV) analysis confirms project viability without policy support (86.2 M$ NPV, 19-year payback), with carbon pricing providing superior long-term value over production subsidies. The results highlight the strong potential of Gen3 CSP–SOEC systems for dispatchable green hydrogen production in moderate-DNI regions, leveraging mature sodium receiver technology.

Experimental assessment of rotational speed stability in a micro turbojet engine for unmanned aerial vehicles based on fuel physicochemical properties, engine performance, and vibration analysis
abstract: This study investigated the rotational speed stability of a micro turbojet engine operating with three different fuels through physicochemical fuel characterization, engine performance testing, and vibration-based stability analysis. Experiments were conducted on a micro turbojet engine used in unmanned aerial vehicle applications under five steady-state operating regimes. Key performance parameters—including thrust, turbine inlet temperature, fuel flow rate, and specific fuel consumption—were investigated. Engine stability was evaluated using two triaxial accelerometers installed near the compressor and turbine bearing planes, while rotational speed variations were analyzed from vibration signals and encoder measurements using short-time Fourier transform, root mean square, and kurtosis indicators. The results showed that diesel fuel containing 5 vol% lubricating oil provided engine performance comparable to Jet A containing 5 vol% lubricating oil, with thrust and fuel flow variations generally below 3%. In contrast, biodiesel containing 5 vol% lubricating oil increased the specific fuel consumption by up to 17%. For all tested fuel–lubricating-oil formulations, kurtosis values remained below 3, indicating no pronounced impulsive or shock-like behavior in the measured vibration signals. However, at high operating regimes (approximately 110000 rpm), biodiesel and diesel fuel containing 5 vol% lubricating oil produced slightly higher vibration amplitudes than Jet A containing 5 vol% lubricating oil. The standard deviation and coefficient of variation ranged from 27 rpm to 869 rpm and 0.06% to 2.01% for engine speed, from 0.11 N to 0.78 N and 0.59% to 7.89% for thrust force, and from 0.07 L/h to 0.20 L/h and 0.38% to 2.91% for volumetric fuel flow rate, respectively. Overall, the diesel fuel formulation containing lubricating oil exhibited performance and vibration characteristics closest to those of Jet A formulation containing lubricating oil under the investigated conditions, while the biodiesel formulation containing lubricating oil resulted in higher fuel consumption and slightly increased vibration amplitudes at high operating regimes. These findings are limited to the short-duration operating conditions investigated in the present study.

Public attitudes and actions towards renewable energy in the EU countries: A micro-level analysis during the energy crisis
abstract: The paper examines the factors affecting individuals' attitudes towards renewable energy (RE) and their willingness to adopt it. It particularly explores the consequences of changes in energy prices during the EU energy crisis. The study considers both socioeconomic and financial factors as well as non-economic factors. Based on the existing research, this study offers novel empirical insights into the economic aspects and decision-making related to RE usage. The analysis uses micro-level data from the Flash Eurobarometer, with approximately 23,000 respondents across EU countries. To ensure robust results, a combination of statistical and machine learning methods is employed. Classification trees and random forests complement logistic regression results by exploring interconnections in people's attitudes and predicting potential actions. Our results allow us to make recommendations for EU energy policy. We highlighted the effects of energy prices and socio-economic factors on households' decision to adopt RE. Our results suggest the existence of a significant Attitude-Behaviour gap as well as an inverse Attitude-Behaviour gap for some cohorts. Policies to support the adoption of RE should address the identified differences and include tools to reduce costs and support regions with high energy prices and high energy demand, as well as certain cohorts, such as the elderly population and job seekers.

Benchmarking heuristics and deterministic optimization with and without warm-starting for district heating network design
abstract: This study develops three heuristics for district heating network design, each capable of handling multiple design periods and heat sources, and systematically benchmarks them alongside deterministic global optimization methods on 56 real-world districts with up to 10000 heat sinks. The benchmarked models include mixed-integer linear programs (MILPs) with affine and constant regression models, a linear programming model with a linear regression, minimum and prize-collecting Steiner tree heuristics, and a constrained Steiner tree. Two design scenarios are considered: forced design, in which all sinks must be connected, and economic design, in which profitability determines which sinks under a given heat price are connected. A key focus of this study is investigating how MILP optimizations for district heating networks can be warm-started using heuristic solutions and the resulting impact on computational time. In the forced design scenario, warm-starting reduces the time to solve the constant regression model by approximately 24% on average, extending the maximum solvable district size from 4750 to 7750 sinks. In the economic design scenario, warm-starting proves especially effective for refining solutions in smaller districts while still yielding improvements in larger districts with more than \num{4000} heat sinks. Across both scenarios, the affine and constant regression MILP models consistently deliver the best network designs, while the linear regression model performs the worst compared to the investigated heuristics. Overall, fast heuristics are recommended for large districts or early-stage planning, while warm-started MILP optimization is recommended for later planning stages.

Renewable Energy-Supplemented Framework for Mitigating Power Supply Interruption and Carbon Emission Issues in MSMEs
abstract: Intermittent power supply and rising carbon emissions have become global challenges for operations management planners because they degrade resource performance and ecological balance. However, the organization uses several energy supply equipment and plans to minimize power outages and toxic pollutants. Micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) are more likely to fail because their operations require high power. Operations planning individuals emphasising the use of renewable energy sources (RES) to strengthen the power supply system and reduce carbon emissions. The study proposed a renewable energy-supplemented framework to address power supply interruptions and reduce carbon emissions in the current organisational landscape. The framework is verified by applying it over seven days to a real-life work scenario. The organization department addresses the needs of various manufactured products in related departments and sections. The current study thoroughly analysed operations management over the year, utilising both traditional and advanced concepts. Afterwards, the study implemented appropriate amendments under the identified conditions to mitigate the issues. The study verified the amendments' suitability by reviewing energy consumption records over the next 7 days. The results showed improvements in operators' contributions, machinery utilization, and idle time by 40%, 28.57%, and 48.67%, respectively. The study reported a reduction of 22,464 kWh in energy, Rs 1,68,483.4 in electricity costs, and 16,174.41 kg CO 2 in carbon emissions over one year. Statistical validation confirmed the stability of these improvements across the monitoring period, with narrow 95% confidence intervals and low day-level variability. The study provides an executive plan for improving power supply reliability and reducing carbon footprints to support Sustainable Development Goals 7, 9, 12, and 13 in MSMEs.

Unified Framework for the Assessment of Rooftop Solar PV Electricity Generation Potential in EU-27
abstract: Achieving climate neutrality in European cities requires large-scale deployment of renewable energy, with solar photovoltaics (PV) expected to play a central role under EU initiatives such as the European Green Deal, REPowerEU, and NetZero Cities. Although rooftop PV potential has been examined in individual cities, differences in data sources and methodological assumptions hinder direct comparison across Europe, and a harmonized assessment covering all 27 EU capital cities remains lacking. This study fills that gap by applying a unified framework integrating Copernicus urban datasets, a 16-year climatological record (2008–2023), and PVGIS performance simulations. The effects of urban shading, cloud cover, and aerosol loading are quantified separately through three modification factors (SMF, CMF, AMF), enabling explicit attribution of irradiance losses across cities. Exploitable rooftop area ranges from 2.6 km 2 in Valletta to 72.2 km 2 in Paris, translating into annual generation potential of 0.2 TWh to 3.8 TWh respectively. Obtained estimates suggest that rooftop PV can meet or exceed household electricity demand in cities such as Luxembourg (180%), however data across the EU capitals indicates that there is an empirical ceiling of 35% for rooftop PV as a standalone measure. Annual avoided CO 2 emissions may reach up to approximately 1 million tCO 2 e, while net economic revenues may exceed 330 MEUR current market values s. The findings propose a harmonized approach yielding metrics that support a differentiated approach to urban solar policy, identifying where rooftop PV can make a major contribution to local electricity supply and where complementary measures remain necessary.

Life cycle assessment of waste-derived hydrochar heating and flue-gas CO2 utilisation in greenhouse crop production
abstract: ABSTRACT Greenhouse crop production requires thermal energy for climate control, generating greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions when fossil fuels are used. CO 2 enrichment can increase crop productivity, but its climate-change performance depends on the CO 2 source and gas treatment required before greenhouse use. This study assesses an integrated 0e-MISION system combining organic-residue valorisation by hydrothermal carbonisation, hydrochar-based heat supply, flue-gas biofiltration and CO 2 fertilisation. A cradle-to-greenhouse-gate life cycle assessment was conducted using 1 kg of marketable crop as functional unit. Tomato, cucumber and strawberry were assessed using CO 2 -enrichment responses from the supporting experimental study. Hydrochars from organic fraction of municipal solid waste (OFMSW) and pruning-waste were compared with natural gas and wood-pellet reference scenarios including conventional management of equivalent residues. The 0e-MISION scenario reduced GHG emissions by 71-78% relative to natural gas under the assumptions tested. Under the multifunctional baseline scenario, it also showed 24-40% lower GHG emissions than the wood-pellet reference; however, this comparison was conditional on conventional management of equivalent organic-residue flows in the references. When these burdens were excluded, the advantage over wood pellets was lost, and 0e-MISION showed 75-145% higher climate-change impacts than the wood pellets. The main hotspot was flue-gas biofiltration, associated with electricity and material inputs. Replacing grid electricity with photovoltaic electricity for biofilter operation reduced impacts by 31-32% for OFMSW hydrochar and 27-28% for pruning-waste hydrochar. Yield-response sensitivity confirmed a robust advantage over natural gas, whereas the comparison with wood pellets depended on maintaining part of the CO 2 -induced yield benefit and multifunctional residue-management framing.
